title: Muscles in pairs, joints, and skeletons of shell and water: how muscles that can only pull move a body

summary.text: A muscle can only pull. It can never push. So how do you push your tongue out of your mouth? In this lesson you will roll a dough worm to find how much longer a body gets when it is squeezed thinner. You will find the partner of each muscle, hunt for six kinds of joint, and measure how high each finger can lift alone. Then you will see how a crab moves inside armour, and how an earthworm moves with a skeleton made of water.
summary.art: A girl sticking her tongue out at a mirror while rolling a long rope of chapati dough on a steel plate, with a ruler beside it and an earthworm drawn in her notebook.

intro.hook: Bend your arm. A muscle pulled it. Now stick out your tongue. No muscle can push. So what moved your tongue forward, out of your mouth?
intro.text: Every muscle in every animal works in one way. It gets shorter, and so it pulls. It cannot push, and it cannot make itself long again. Your arm has bones for muscles to pull on. Your tongue has no bone at all, and neither has an earthworm. Yet a tongue can reach out and an earthworm can stretch forward. By the end of this lesson you will be able to say exactly how they do it.
intro.art: A split picture: on one side a child's bent arm with the upper-arm muscle bulging, on the other the same child with her tongue stretched out, and a question mark between them.

outcomes: I can explain why a muscle can only pull, using the sliding threads inside a muscle fibre.
I can explain why muscles work in antagonistic pairs, and find the partner of a muscle on my own body.
I can name six kinds of moving joint, find each on my body, and say how each one moves.
I can say what cartilage, synovial fluid, ligaments and tendons each do.
I can explain how an animal with an exoskeleton moves and grows, and what moulting costs.
I can explain how a hydrostatic skeleton works, and why a body that gets thinner must get longer.
I can explain how a tongue, an elephant's trunk and an octopus's arm move with no bone.
I can run a fair test, and say what I thought, what I saw and why I think it happened.

terms.meaning: To get shorter. When a muscle contracts, it pulls on whatever it is joined to.
terms.example: Your biceps contracts when you lift a tumbler to your mouth.
terms.art: An upper arm drawn twice: once with a long thin muscle, once with the same muscle short and fat, pulling the forearm up.

terms.meaning: Two muscles that pull in opposite ways across the same joint. Each one stretches the other back to its long shape.
terms.example: The biceps bends your elbow. The triceps straightens it. They are an antagonistic pair.
terms.art: An arm with one muscle on the front coloured red and one on the back coloured blue, with arrows pulling opposite ways.

terms.meaning: A muscle that bends a joint.
terms.example: The biceps is the flexor of the elbow.
terms.art: A bent elbow with the muscle on the inside of the bend coloured.

terms.meaning: A muscle that straightens a joint.
terms.example: The triceps is the extensor of the elbow.
terms.art: A straight arm with the muscle on the back of the upper arm coloured.

terms.meaning: One muscle cell. It is long and very thin, and a muscle is a bundle of thousands of them.
terms.example: Pull a thread from a piece of cooked chicken, or look at the strings in the flesh of a cooked fish. Each thread is a bundle of muscle fibres.
terms.art: A muscle cut across to show bundles inside bundles, with one hair-thin fibre pulled out and labelled.

terms.meaning: Two kinds of protein thread inside every muscle fibre. Myosin threads grab actin threads and pull them along.
terms.example: When you make a fist, countless myosin threads in your forearm are pulling on actin threads.
terms.art: Two sets of threads lying side by side, thick ones with tiny arms reaching to thin ones, drawn far apart and then pulled closer.

terms.meaning: A small molecule that cells use to carry energy from food to wherever work is done. Its full name is adenosine triphosphate.
terms.example: A myosin thread uses one ATP each time it lets go of actin and reaches for a new grip.
terms.art: A tiny three-part token being handed to a small arm on a thick thread, which then lets go of the thin thread.

terms.meaning: A tough cord that joins a muscle to a bone.
terms.example: Press the back of your hand and wiggle your fingers. The cords that move under the skin are tendons.
terms.art: The back of a hand with four cords running from the wrist to the fingers.

terms.meaning: A tough band that joins one bone to another bone at a joint.
terms.example: Ligaments at the sides of your knee stop it from bending sideways.
terms.art: A knee joint seen from the front, with short bands tying the thigh bone to the shin bone on each side.

terms.meaning: A smooth, firm, slightly springy material that covers the ends of bones in a joint.
terms.example: The shiny white cap on the end of a chicken leg bone is cartilage. The tip of your nose is cartilage too.
terms.art: The rounded end of a bone with a smooth pale cap over it, shown beside a nose and an ear in outline.

terms.meaning: A slippery liquid inside a moving joint. It lets the cartilage surfaces slide and it carries food to the cartilage.
terms.example: A healthy knee holds only a little synovial fluid, and that is enough to keep the joint sliding.
terms.art: A joint cut open to show two capped bone ends with a thin layer of liquid between them, inside a closed bag.

terms.meaning: A joint where one bone turns round, like a key in a lock.
terms.example: The joint at the top of your neck lets your head turn to say no.
terms.art: A ring of bone turning round a peg of bone at the top of a neck.

terms.meaning: A joint where two bone ends are each shaped like a saddle and sit across each other. It bends two ways.
terms.example: The joint at the base of your thumb is a saddle joint. It lets your thumb touch each fingertip.
terms.art: Two saddle shapes sitting across each other at the base of a thumb.

terms.meaning: A skeleton on the outside of the body. The muscles are inside it.
terms.example: A crab, a prawn, an ant and a cockroach each have an exoskeleton.
terms.art: A crab leg cut open like a tube, showing muscles inside the hard shell.

terms.meaning: A tough, light material that insects, spiders, crabs and prawns make. Their exoskeleton is built mostly from chitin.
terms.example: The thin clear shell you peel off a prawn is mostly chitin.
terms.art: A peeled prawn shell held up to the light, thin and clear.

terms.meaning: Shedding an old exoskeleton and growing a larger one. An animal in armour can grow only by moulting.
terms.example: The empty brown skin of a cicada on a tree trunk was left behind after a moult.
terms.art: An empty split insect skin holding on to bark, with the pale new insect beside it.

terms.meaning: A skeleton made of liquid shut inside the body. Muscles squeeze the liquid, and the liquid pushes back.
terms.example: An earthworm has a hydrostatic skeleton. Each segment of their body is a small bag of liquid wrapped in muscle.
terms.art: An earthworm cut across to show a ring of muscle round a space full of liquid.

terms.meaning: A body part made almost entirely of muscle, with no bone and no space of liquid. The muscle itself is the skeleton.
terms.example: Your tongue, an elephant's trunk and an octopus's arm are muscular hydrostats.
terms.art: A tongue, an elephant's trunk and an octopus arm drawn side by side, each cut across to show only muscle inside.

terms.meaning: A wave of squeezing that travels along a body or a tube.
terms.example: An earthworm moves forward by peristalsis. Your food pipe moves food down by peristalsis too.
terms.art: An earthworm drawn in three stages, with a thin stretched part moving from the head towards the tail.

explanations.definition: A muscle works by contracting, which means getting shorter. A muscle that gets shorter pulls. No muscle can push, and no muscle can make itself long again.
explanations.description: This is true of every muscle in every animal, from an ant's leg to an elephant's trunk. The reason is inside the muscle. A muscle is made of threads that slide past each other to make it shorter. The threads can pull themselves together. They have no way to push themselves apart. So after a muscle has contracted, something else must pull it long again. That something is usually another muscle. It can also be gravity, a springy band, or liquid under pressure. The rest of this lesson is about the different ways bodies solve this one problem.
examples: Your biceps pulls your forearm up. It cannot push the forearm down again.
A rope works the same way. You can pull a bucket up from a well with a rope, but you cannot push the bucket down with the rope.
Your heart is a muscle. It squeezes blood out by getting shorter all round. Blood coming back in stretches it again.
explanations.art: A hand pulling a bucket up on a rope beside an arm muscle pulling a forearm up, with the word 'pull' on both.

explanations.concept: Inside a muscle: threads that slide
explanations.definition: A muscle fibre is packed with two kinds of protein thread, called actin and myosin. A muscle contracts when the myosin threads pull the actin threads past them. The threads do not shrink. They slide.
explanations.description: Each myosin thread has many tiny arms. An arm grabs the actin thread beside it and bends, which drags the actin along a tiny distance. Then the arm lets go, reaches forward and grabs again. Millions of arms do this many times a second, and the whole fibre gets shorter. The energy comes from ATP, a small molecule that every cell makes from food. Here is a surprise. The arm needs ATP to let go, not only to pull. If ATP runs out, the arms stay locked on. That is why the body of an animal goes stiff a few hours after death. The muscles have no ATP left, so they cannot let go. The stiffness passes later, when the threads themselves begin to break down. Muscle work also gives off heat. That is why you feel warm after running, and why you shiver when you are cold. Shivering is muscles contracting quickly to make heat.
examples: When a muscle contracts, the actin and myosin threads overlap more. Each thread stays the same length.
Letting go costs energy. A myosin arm cannot release its grip until a fresh ATP arrives.
Gerty Cori and Carl Cori worked out how muscles and the liver pass fuel between them. In 1947 Gerty Cori became the first woman to win the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
explanations.art: Thick threads with tiny bent arms gripping thin threads, drawn in two frames: threads overlapping a little, then overlapping a lot, with the threads themselves the same length in both.

explanations.concept: Antagonistic pairs: every muscle needs a partner
explanations.definition: An antagonistic pair is two muscles that pull in opposite ways across the same joint. When one contracts, it moves the bone and also stretches the other back to its long shape.
explanations.description: The flexor bends the joint and the extensor straightens it. At the elbow, the flexor is the biceps and the extensor is the triceps. At the knee, the muscles on the front of the thigh straighten the leg and the muscles on the back of the thigh bend it. The partners do not simply take turns. When your brain tells the biceps to pull, nerve cells in your spinal cord tell the triceps to relax at the same moment. If both pull at once, the joint goes stiff. You do this on purpose when you hold your arm rigid. Sometimes the partner is not a muscle. When you lower a full tumbler slowly, gravity is straightening your elbow. Your biceps is still working, letting the arm down a little at a time. So a muscle can be working while it is getting longer.
examples: Elbow: the biceps bends it, and the triceps straightens it.
Knee: the front thigh muscles straighten it, and the back thigh muscles bend it.
Ankle: the calf muscle points the foot down, and the shin muscle lifts the foot up.
Lowering a bucket into a well slowly: the same arm muscles that lift it are working to let it down.
explanations.art: An arm drawn twice. In one the front muscle is short and the back muscle is long. In the other the back muscle is short and the front muscle is long.

explanations.definition: A joint is a place where two bones meet. The shape of the bone ends decides how the joint can move. There are six main kinds of moving joint.
explanations.description: A hinge joint bends one way and back, like a door. Your elbow, your knee and the joints in your fingers are hinges. A ball and socket joint has a ball on one bone in a cup on the other, so it can swing in a full circle. Your shoulder and your hip are of this kind. A pivot joint lets one bone turn round. One pivot at the top of your neck turns your head. Another near your elbow turns your palm up and down. A saddle joint bends two ways, and the base of your thumb has one. An ellipsoid joint is an oval knob in an oval cup. It bends two ways but cannot spin, and your wrist is one. A gliding joint has flat surfaces that slide a little, as between the small bones of your wrist and ankle. Some joints do not move at all. The plates of your skull are locked together by zigzag joints called sutures. There is a price for free movement. A joint that can swing every way, like the shoulder, has to be held in place mostly by muscles and ligaments, and not by the fit of the bones.
examples: Hinge: elbow, knee, finger joints.
Ball and socket: shoulder, hip.
Pivot: turning the head, turning the palm.
Saddle: base of the thumb.
Ellipsoid: wrist, knuckles.
Gliding: between the small bones of the wrist and the ankle.
explanations.art: Six small drawings in a row, each showing a joint beside an everyday object: a door hinge, a ball in a cup, a key in a lock, a rider on a saddle, an egg in a spoon and two flat tiles sliding.

explanations.concept: Inside a moving joint: cartilage, fluid and ligaments
explanations.definition: In a moving joint, the bone ends are capped with smooth cartilage. The joint is closed in a bag that holds slippery synovial fluid. Ligaments tie bone to bone.
explanations.description: Bone rubbing on bone would wear out quickly. Cartilage on cartilage, wetted with synovial fluid, slides with very little friction. Friction is the grip between two surfaces that rub. The fluid has a second job. Cartilage has no blood vessels of its own, so it takes its food from the fluid. This is one reason a damaged cartilage heals slowly and poorly. Ligaments are tough bands that hold the bones together and stop the joint from bending the wrong way. A sprain is a ligament that has been stretched too far or torn. Tendons, ligaments and cartilage all get their strength from a protein called collagen. Collagen is a rope of three strands twisted together. In 1954 G. N. Ramachandran and Gopinath Kartha, at the University of Madras, worked out this twisted rope of three strands. Their model, with later corrections, still stands.
examples: The white shiny cap on a chicken leg bone is cartilage.
A twisted ankle hurts for weeks because a ligament has been overstretched.
Collagen's rope of three strands was worked out in Madras, which is now Chennai, in 1954.
explanations.art: A knee joint cut open from the side, showing two bone ends with pale caps, a thin layer of fluid between them, a bag round the joint and bands at the sides.

explanations.concept: Muscles can be far from the part they move
explanations.definition: A muscle does not have to sit beside the part it moves. A long tendon can carry its pull to a bone far away.
explanations.description: Your fingers hold almost no muscle. The muscles that bend and straighten them are in your forearm. Long tendons run from those muscles, through the wrist, to the finger bones. You can see the tendons move on the back of your hand. This keeps the fingers thin and light, so they can move quickly. It also means that some fingers are tied together. The tendons that straighten the middle, ring and little fingers are joined to each other by small bands on the back of the hand. And some of the muscles in the forearm send tendons to more than one finger. So your ring finger cannot move fully by itself. Scientists have found that these links in the hand are a main reason, and that the way the brain controls the muscles adds to it.
examples: Grip your forearm near the elbow and wiggle your fingers. You can feel the finger muscles working there.
Lay your hand flat and try to lift only the ring finger. It lifts less than the others.
The index finger and the little finger each have an extra muscle of their own for straightening. The ring finger has none.
explanations.art: A forearm and hand with the skin shown clear, muscles bunched near the elbow and long thin cords running through the wrist to the fingertips.

explanations.concept: An exoskeleton: muscles inside a tube
explanations.definition: An animal with an exoskeleton has a hard skeleton on the outside, and the muscles are inside it. The muscles still work in antagonistic pairs.
explanations.description: Insects, spiders, crabs and prawns are arthropods. An arthropod is an animal with a hard outer covering and jointed legs. The covering is made mostly of chitin. In crabs and prawns it is hardened further with minerals from the sea. Each leg is a row of hard tubes. Between the tubes the covering is thin and soft, and that soft part is the joint. Inside each tube are a flexor muscle and an extensor muscle. They are fixed to the inside of the shell, often on flat plates that grow inwards from it. If your family eats crab, you may have pulled a flat white blade out of a claw. That blade is one of these plates, and the muscle that closes the claw was fixed to it. A hollow tube is a good shape for a small animal. It is light and stiff, and it is armour as well as skeleton.
examples: A crab's claw has a big muscle to close it and a small muscle to open it. Both are inside the claw.
An ant's leg is a row of hard tubes with soft joints between them.
The coconut crab is the largest arthropod living on land. A big one weighs about 4 kilograms. Coconut crabs have been recorded on India's Nicobar Islands.
explanations.art: A crab claw drawn as if made of glass, with a large muscle and a small muscle inside it, each fixed to a flat plate that leads to the moving finger of the claw.

explanations.definition: A hard exoskeleton cannot grow. So an arthropod grows by moulting. The animal sheds the old exoskeleton and swells up before the new one hardens.
explanations.description: Before a moult, the animal grows a new soft exoskeleton under the old one. The old one splits, and the animal climbs out. Then they take in water or air and swell, so that the new covering hardens at a larger size. For hours or days the new covering is soft. In that time the animal cannot move well, because soft tubes bend when the muscles pull on them. The animal also has no armour. Many arthropods hide while this lasts. So an outside skeleton has a cost that an inside skeleton does not have. An animal with bones grows without ever losing the use of the skeleton.
examples: The empty cicada skins on tree trunks in the rainy season are old exoskeletons.
A crab who has just moulted is soft all over and hides until the shell hardens.
A caterpillar moults several times before becoming a pupa.
explanations.art: A cicada half out of a split brown skin on a tree trunk, pale and soft, with wings still crumpled.

explanations.concept: A spider's leg: a muscle on one side, liquid pressure on the other
explanations.definition: At two of the main joints in a spider's leg there is a flexor muscle and no extensor muscle. The leg is straightened by the pressure of the spider's blood.
explanations.description: This was shown in 1959 by two scientists in Cambridge, D. A. Parry and R. H. J. Brown. They measured the pressure of the liquid inside spiders' legs and found that it rises when the legs straighten. So at these joints the partner of the flexor muscle is not another muscle. It is liquid, pushed into the leg by muscles in the front part of the spider's body. This explains something you may have seen. The legs of a dead spider are curled in. With no pressure in the liquid, nothing holds the legs out against the pull of the flexors. Later work has found that in some large spiders, springy parts of the joint help as well.
examples: Parry and Brown also argued that a small jumping spider leaps by a sudden rise of pressure in the back legs. Later studies of larger jumping spiders disagree about how much the leg muscles add.
A dead spider has curled legs, because the pressure that held them straight is gone.
Here the antagonistic pair is a muscle and a liquid.
explanations.art: A spider's leg drawn in two frames, bent with a small muscle pulling inside the joint, and straight with arrows showing liquid pressing outward inside the leg.

explanations.definition: A hydrostatic skeleton is liquid shut inside a body and wrapped in muscle. The liquid cannot be squeezed into less space, so when muscles squeeze it one way, it pushes out another way.
explanations.description: An earthworm's body is a row of ringed segments, and a large earthworm has more than a hundred of them. Thin walls separate the segments, and each one is a closed bag of liquid. Two sets of muscles wrap each segment. Circular muscles go round it like a ring, so they are also called ring muscles. Longitudinal muscles run along it from front to back, so they are also called lengthwise muscles. When the circular muscles contract, the segment gets thinner. The liquid has to go somewhere, so the segment gets longer. That lengthening stretches the longitudinal muscles. When the longitudinal muscles contract, the segment gets shorter and fatter, and that stretches the circular muscles. So the two sets are an antagonistic pair, and the liquid between them does the job that a bone does in your arm. To move, the worm sends a wave of thinning and fattening along their body. Tiny bristles on the fat segments grip the soil, so the thin segments can push forward. In the Dough Worm experiment you find how much longer a body gets when it is squeezed thinner.
examples: Circular muscles contract: the segment gets long and thin.
Longitudinal muscles contract: the segment gets short and fat.
Sea anemones, jellyfish and many worms also have hydrostatic skeletons.
A caterpillar is an insect with a soft body. Their body is held firm by liquid under pressure.
explanations.art: An earthworm in soil with some segments long and thin and others short and fat, and a close-up ring showing circular muscle outside, lengthwise muscle inside and liquid in the middle.

explanations.concept: A tongue, a trunk and an octopus arm: muscle that is its own skeleton
explanations.definition: A muscular hydrostat is a body part made almost entirely of muscle. It has no bone and no bag of liquid. The muscle itself keeps the same volume, and so it acts as its own skeleton.
explanations.description: Muscle is mostly water, and water keeps its volume when it is squeezed. Volume is the amount of space a thing takes up. In a tongue, muscle fibres run in three directions: along it, across it, and from top to bottom. When the fibres that run across and from top to bottom contract, the tongue gets narrower and thinner. Its volume cannot change, so it must get longer. This is how you stick your tongue out. No muscle pushes it. Muscles pull it thin, and the thinning makes it long. A muscle from your chin to the tongue also pulls the back of the tongue forward. To pull the tongue in, the fibres that run along it contract. William Kier and Kathleen Smith described this in 1985. They showed that tongues, the arms and tentacles of octopuses and squid, and the trunks of elephants all work this way. A human tongue has eight muscles. An elephant's trunk has about 90,000 small bundles of muscle, counted in 2023 from scans of the trunk of a baby Asian elephant.
examples: Stick your tongue out: it becomes narrower and thinner as it gets longer.
An elephant can pick up a single peanut or lift a log with the same trunk.
An octopus can bend her arm at any point along it, because the arm has no bones to limit it.
explanations.art: A tongue, an elephant's trunk and an octopus arm, each drawn short and fat and then long and thin, with the same amount of colour filling both shapes.

explanations.concept: Thinner by half, longer by four
explanations.definition: When a body of fixed volume is squeezed to half its width, it does not get twice as long. It gets about four times as long.
explanations.description: You measure this yourself in the Dough Worm experiment. The reason is that a round body is narrow in two directions at once, from side to side and from top to bottom. Halving the width halves both. So the same amount of stuff has to spread along four times the length. This is why muscular hydrostats can be so quick. A small squeeze across gives a large movement along. A squid shoots out her two long tentacles to catch a prawn in a small fraction of a second, by squeezing them thinner. The rule is exact only for a perfect cylinder, which is a shape like a tumbler or a pipe. Real tongues and worms are close to it, but not exact.
examples: A dough roll 4 centimetres wide and 4 centimetres long becomes about 16 centimetres long when rolled to 2 centimetres wide.
A tongue that gets only a little narrower and thinner reaches out a long way.
It works backwards too. A worm segment that shortens a little gets much fatter, and grips the burrow wall.
explanations.art: Three dough rolls made from equal lumps, one short and wide, one four times as long and half as wide, and one very long and thin, with a ruler under them.

explanations.definition: Soft parts of a plant are held up by water pressing outward inside each cell. A plant with too little water wilts, because that pressure falls.
explanations.description: A plant cell is a small box with a firm wall, full of watery liquid. When the cell is full, the liquid presses on the wall, and the cell is stiff. Thousands of stiff cells make a leaf stand out flat. When the plant loses more water than their roots take in, the cells go slack and the leaf droops. Plants have no muscles, but some plants move by using this pressure. A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves when touched. At the base of each leaf is a small swelling. Cells on one side of the swelling let water out quickly, that side goes slack, and the leaf folds. So a plant can move by changing a water skeleton, with no muscle at all.
examples: Coriander left out on the kitchen counter droops. Stood in water, the stalks rise again.
A touch-me-not plant folds their leaves in about a second.
A crisp cucumber is crisp because the cells are full of water under pressure.
explanations.art: A sprig of coriander drawn twice, drooping on a counter and standing up in a tumbler of water, with a close-up of slack cells and full cells.

explanations.concept: Why are there no giant insects on land?
explanations.description: The largest land arthropod alive, the coconut crab, weighs about 4 kilograms. The largest insects weigh far less. Nobody has a single agreed answer for why. Several ideas are being tested, and more than one may be true.
examples: About 300 million years ago there were insects like giant dragonflies, with wings about 70 centimetres from tip to tip.
In the sea, where water holds a body up, crabs and lobsters grow much larger than any land insect.

perspectives.explanation: Insects breathe through fine air tubes that run to every part of the body. In 2007 Alexander Kaiser and others measured beetles of many sizes with X-rays. They found that bigger beetles give a larger share of the body to air tubes. They argued that in a giant insect the tubes would leave too little room in the legs.

In 2026 a study of 44 kinds of living insects reported that the finest air tubes take up very little room at every body size. Its authors argue that oxygen supply is not what stops insects from being giants.
A freshly moulted arthropod is soft. On land, a very heavy soft body would sag under its own weight before the new skeleton hardened. In water the body is held up, so this problem is smaller.
Large insects are easy food for birds and bats, who fly better and are warm-blooded. On this view insects stay small because the place of the large flying animal is already taken.

explanations.art: A beetle on a child's palm beside a faint outline of the same beetle drawn as big as a dog, with a question mark.

agreed.text: Muscles contract by threads sliding past each other. The threads themselves do not shorten.
agreed.evidence: In 1954 two teams looked at working muscle under new kinds of microscope. Both saw that the dark bands, where the thick threads lie, stay the same width while the muscle shortens. Later pictures from electron microscopes showed the two sets of threads and the tiny arms between them.

agreed.text: A muscle fibre can pull but cannot push, so every movement needs something to pull the muscle long again.
agreed.evidence: Every muscle that has been studied works against an opposing muscle, a springy part, gravity or liquid under pressure. In the laboratory, a muscle fibre that has shortened has to be drawn out again by a weight or a spring.

agreed.text: Letting go needs energy. A myosin arm cannot release actin without ATP.
agreed.evidence: Muscle fibres kept in a dish with no ATP go stiff and stay stiff. Adding ATP makes them soften again. The stiffness of a body after death has the same cause.

agreed.text: The shape of the bone ends decides how a joint can move.
agreed.evidence: Skeletons, X-ray pictures and scans show a ball in a cup at every shoulder and hip, and a hinge at every elbow. A hinge joint in any person swings one way only.

agreed.text: Tongues, trunks and octopus arms move without bones because muscle keeps its volume.
agreed.evidence: William Kier and Kathleen Smith compared the muscles of tongues, tentacles and trunks in 1985. In each they found fibres running in several directions, and they showed that a change in width must give a change in length.

agreed.text: Arthropods can grow only by moulting, and they are soft and slow just after a moult.
agreed.evidence: Moulting has been watched and filmed in crabs, prawns, cicadas, cockroaches and spiders. Fishers have long known that a crab with a soft shell has just moulted.

challenging.claim: Muscles push as well as pull.
challenging.for: We do push doors, carts and swings, and it feels as if our arms push.
challenging.against: When you push a door, your triceps is pulling on your forearm bone, and the bone pushes the door. Bones and liquids can push. Muscle threads can only slide together.
challenging.context: This card is about what a muscle can and cannot do.

challenging.claim: A relaxed muscle is using no energy, and only pulling costs energy.
challenging.against: A myosin arm needs ATP to let go of actin. A signal from a nerve releases calcium inside the fibre, and the calcium switches the muscle on. The cell uses more ATP to pump that calcium away again. A muscle with no ATP cannot relax. It goes stiff.
challenging.context: This card is about whether letting go is free.

challenging.claim: A skeleton has to be hard.
challenging.who: A common belief, and the usual meaning of the word
challenging.for: Our own skeleton is bone, and the word 'skeleton' makes most people think of bones.
challenging.against: Earthworms, sea anemones and caterpillars move with a skeleton of liquid. A tongue and a trunk move with a skeleton of muscle. What makes something a skeleton is the job it does for the muscles.
challenging.context: This card is about what counts as a skeleton.

challenging.claim: Your ring finger moves poorly because its muscle is weak.
challenging.for: The ring finger does feel weaker when you try to lift it alone.
challenging.against: Studies of hands show that the fingers are tied together by links between their tendons, and that some forearm muscles serve several fingers. The way the brain drives these muscles adds to the effect. A weak muscle is not the main cause.
challenging.context: This card is about why one finger cannot move fully by itself.

challenging.claim: Animals with soft bodies are simpler than animals with bones.
challenging.who: An old view in many textbooks
challenging.for: A worm looks plain beside a cat, and a soft body has fewer parts with names.
challenging.against: A bony arm bends only at its joints. An octopus's arm can bend, twist, shorten and lengthen at any point. Controlling it is a harder problem, and engineers who build soft robots study octopus arms and elephant trunks to learn how.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a body with no bones is a simple body.

challenging.claim: Insects are small because oxygen cannot reach the inside of a big insect.
challenging.for: Insects breathe through air tubes. A 2007 X-ray study found that bigger beetles give more of the body to tubes. Giant insects lived when the air held more oxygen.
challenging.against: A 2026 study of 44 kinds of insect found that the finest tubes take very little room at any size. Moulting, weight, and being hunted by birds and bats may matter as much or more.
challenging.context: This card is about why no insect is as big as a dog.

big_questions.q: Your biceps bends your arm, but only because your triceps stretched it first. So which muscle bends your arm?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the biceps could do if nothing ever pulled it long again.

big_questions.q: Is the liquid inside an earthworm part of their skeleton, or is it only liquid?
big_questions.hint: Ask what job a bone does for your muscles, and whether the liquid does the same job.

big_questions.q: Your tongue has no bone. Is your tongue a muscle, or a skeleton, or both?
big_questions.hint: Remember what happens to its length when it is squeezed thinner.

big_questions.q: A myosin arm needs energy to let go. In your own life, is letting go ever work?
big_questions.hint: Think of putting down a heavy bag slowly, or relaxing your shoulders when you are tense.

big_questions.q: A crab must become soft and helpless in order to grow. Could anything grow without a risky time like that?
big_questions.hint: Compare a crab's way of growing with the way your own bones grow.

big_questions.q: A plant folds a leaf with no muscle. So what is needed for a living being to move?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the touch-me-not, the earthworm and your arm all use.

story.title: The Net That Would Not Rise
story.note: Ammu, her mother Sosamma, Thresiamma chechi and the crew are made up, and so is this evening. These facts are real. The big shore nets at Fort Kochi in Kerala are called cheenavala, or Chinese fishing nets. Each one is a frame of teak and bamboo about 10 metres high. The crew lower the net by walking out along the main beam. Large stones hang from ropes on the shore side, and the weight of the stones helps to lift the net again. A crew is usually four to six people. Crews at Fort Kochi are almost always men. A crew led by a woman is imagined here.
text: Ammu's mother kept the ropes of the third net at Fort Kochi.

There were six people in the crew, and Sosamma was the only one who never touched a fish. She oiled the pulleys with coconut oil. She checked every knot at low tide. She knew each of the seven stones that hung on the shore side of the net, because she had tied them there herself, each on a rope of a different length.
Ammu was ten, and she had watched the net go down and come up more times than she had eaten breakfast.

It always went the same way. Thresiamma chechi, who led the crew, would call out. Two of the crew would walk along the great beam, out over the water, with their arms spread like people on a wall. Their weight tipped the frame. The net sank into the green water, wide as a house. On the shore side, the seven stones rose into the air, one after another, turning slowly on their ropes.
Then everyone waited. Five minutes, never much more.
Then the two walked back, the crew took hold of the ropes, and the stones came down as the net came up, streaming, with silver things jumping in the bottom of it.
On the evening it went wrong, the sky over the harbour was the colour of a ripe papaya, and a ferry was hooting its way across to Vypin.
The net went down. The stones went up. Ammu was sitting on an upturned boat, eating a boiled egg.
There was a crack like a coconut splitting.

The biggest rope, the one that carried the three heaviest stones, had parted high up near the frame. The three stones dropped straight down and buried themselves to their middles in the wet sand. The frame gave a long groan. It tilted further towards the sea than Ammu had ever seen it tilt, and it stayed there.
"Up!" Thresiamma chechi shouted. "Bring it up!"

The crew threw themselves on the four ropes that were left. They pulled until their feet dug trenches in the sand. The net rose the height of a child, and stopped. It was full. Ammu could see the water inside it shivering with fish.
"It is too heavy," Sosamma said. "Four stones cannot do it."
"Then we push," said Thresiamma chechi.

She and Babu ran under the sea end of the frame with two long bamboo poles. They set the poles against the beam above their heads and pushed. The poles bent like bows. The beam did not move. Babu's pole slipped and went into the harbour like a spear.
"Again!"

They pushed again. Ammu watched their arms shake. She watched the tide, too. It had turned. In half an hour the water would be pulling hard at a full net on a tilted frame, and her mother had told her what happened to the second net in the year Ammu was born.
She looked at the three stones in the sand. She looked up at the four stones still hanging, and at the long beam, and at the net.
It was strange. She had seen it every day of her life, and she had never seen it.

Nothing in the whole frame ever pushed. The crew walking out did not push the net down. Their weight pulled that end down. The stones did not push the net up. They hung on their ropes and pulled the shore end down, and the net end rose because the other end fell. A rope could not push anything. Every rope on the frame pulled, and for every pull one way there was a pull the other way to undo it. Now one of the two pulls was lying in the sand.
Pushing was no use. The frame had never been built to be pushed.
"Amma," she said. "The broken rope. Is the top half still tied to the frame?"
Sosamma looked up. Four metres of rope hung from the beam, swinging, its end frayed like a paintbrush.
"It is."
"Then it does not need the stones," Ammu said. "It only needs to be pulled down. By anything heavy." She was already running. "We are heavy!"

Her mother understood before she had finished the word. Sosamma knotted a loop in the hanging rope as high as she could reach, put her foot in it, and hung there with her whole weight. Ammu jumped and caught the rope above her mother's hands.
The frame creaked.
"More!" Sosamma shouted, not to the crew, but to the sea wall.

There were people on the sea wall, as there were every evening. A woman selling roasted groundnuts. Two college girls with a phone. A man with a child on his shoulders. They had been watching the trouble in the way people watch trouble.

The groundnut seller put down her basket first. She was a broad woman, and when she took hold of the rope and lifted her feet, the beam moved a full hand's width. The college girls came next, laughing and frightened. Then the man, with the child still on his shoulders.
Seven people hung on one rope like fruit on a stalk.
"Now pull!" called Thresiamma chechi, and the crew hauled on the other four.
The net came up out of the harbour, pouring. It came up slowly and all the way, and the frame stood level again against the papaya sky.
Nobody on the rope let go until Sosamma said they could.

Later, when the catch was in baskets and the groundnut seller had been given a seer fish as long as her arm, Ammu went and sat by the three stones in the sand. Her mother was already measuring new rope against her outstretched arms.
"Three days to tie them back," Sosamma said. "You can help. Each on its own length, so they lift one by one."
Ammu put her hand on the biggest stone. It was still warm from the day.
"I always thought the net was the thing that did the work," she said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the story never mentions muscles, but the net works the way a joint does. A rope can only pull, like a muscle. The crew's weight pulls the net down and the stones pull it up again, so the two are an antagonistic pair with the beam between them, as the biceps and triceps are with the forearm between them. When one pull is lost, pushing fails, because nothing in the frame was built to push. Ammu's turn is seeing that the missing pull can be given by anything heavy. Ask your child which part of the net is like a bone, which is like the biceps and which is like the triceps.
ask: A rope can pull but cannot push. Which part of your body works like that?
The net went down by one pull and came up by another. Which pair in your arm does the same?
Why did pushing on the beam with poles fail?
The people on the rope replaced the stones. What could replace a muscle's partner in a body?
What did Ammu mean when she said she had thought the net did the work?

games.title: Pair Up: find the pull that undoes the pull
games.context: This is a memory game about antagonistic pairs. Every card names one pull in a body. Somewhere on the table is the card that undoes it. You find the two and say what carries the pull between them.

printables.title: 24 pull cards, in 12 pairs
items: ELBOW. The biceps contracts. The elbow bends.
ELBOW. The triceps contracts. The elbow straightens.
KNEE. The front thigh muscles contract. The knee straightens.
KNEE. The back thigh muscles contract. The knee bends.
ANKLE. The calf muscle contracts. The foot points down.
ANKLE. The shin muscle contracts. The foot lifts up.
HAND. Muscles on the palm side of the forearm contract. The hand closes.
HAND. Muscles on the back of the forearm contract. The hand opens.
JAW. The chewing muscles of the cheek contract. The mouth shuts.
JAW. The muscles under the chin contract. The mouth opens.
EYELID. A ring of muscle round the eye contracts. The eye shuts.
EYELID. A small muscle above the eye contracts. The lid lifts.
EYE. A ring of muscle in the iris contracts. The pupil gets smaller.
EYE. Muscle fibres set like wheel spokes in the iris contract. The pupil gets bigger.
EARTHWORM. The circular muscles contract. The segment gets long and thin.
EARTHWORM. The longitudinal muscles contract. The segment gets short and fat.
TONGUE. Fibres running across and up-and-down contract. The tongue gets long.
TONGUE. Fibres running along the tongue contract. The tongue gets short.
CRAB CLAW. The big closer muscle inside the claw contracts. The claw shuts.
CRAB CLAW. The small opener muscle inside the claw contracts. The claw opens.
SPIDER LEG. The flexor muscle contracts. The leg bends.
SPIDER LEG. Blood is pushed into the leg under pressure. The leg straightens.
CLAM. The closing muscle contracts. The two shells shut.
CLAM. The closing muscle relaxes. A springy band at the hinge opens the shells.

printables.title: Answer sheet: the 12 pairs, and what carries the pull between them
items: Elbow: biceps and triceps. Bone carries the pull.
Knee: front and back thigh muscles. Bone carries the pull.
Ankle: calf muscle and shin muscle. Bone carries the pull.
Hand: closing and opening muscles in the forearm. Tendons and bones carry the pull.
Jaw: cheek muscles and muscles under the chin. Bone carries the pull.
Eyelid: a ring muscle and a lifting muscle. No bone is between them, only the soft lid.
Iris: ring fibres and spoke fibres. No bone is between them. Each stretches the other directly.
Earthworm: circular and longitudinal muscles. Liquid carries the pull.
Tongue: fibres in different directions. The muscle itself carries the pull.
Crab claw: closer and opener muscles. Shell carries the pull.
Spider leg: a flexor muscle and liquid pressure. The partner is not a muscle.
Clam: a closing muscle and a springy band. The partner is not a muscle.

rules: Shuffle the 24 cards. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 6.
On your turn, turn over any two cards and read them aloud.
If the two cards are the two halves of one pair, say what carries the pull between them: bone, shell, liquid, the muscle itself or a springy band.
Check with the answer sheet. If you are right, keep the pair. If you are wrong, turn both cards back.
If the two cards are not a pair, turn them back in the same places.
The game ends when all 12 pairs are taken. The player with the most pairs wins.
Playing alone, count your turns. Play again and try to finish in fewer turns.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Lay them face down in 4 rows of 6. 4. Keep the answer sheet face down.
flow.say: Every card names one pull in a body. A muscle cannot undo its own pull. So each card has a partner card that undoes it.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Mix them. Lay them face down in rows.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pair Up. You lay out 24 cards that each name one pull in a body.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to turn over two cards. 2. Read both aloud. 3. If they are a pair, say what carries the pull between them. 4. Check the answer sheet.
flow.say: Read both cards. Does one undo the other? What lies between the two pulls: bone, shell, liquid, muscle or a spring?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. Read them aloud. Are they a pair? Say what lies between them.

ask.q: Which pairs on the table have a partner that is not a muscle?
good: The spider leg, where liquid pressure straightens the leg.
The clam, where a springy band opens the shell.

flow.parent: The body part is printed in capitals, so finding the pair is a memory task. The thinking is in the second part: what carries the pull. Accept 'water' for liquid. For the eyelid and the iris, a good answer is 'nothing hard'.
flow.context: This is the main part of Pair Up. You find the two pulls that undo each other and say what carries the pull between them.

flow.do: 1. Count each player's pairs. 2. Lay all 12 pairs out in a row. 3. Sort them by what carries the pull.
flow.say: Sort the pairs. Which use bone? Which use shell? Which use liquid? Which use no hard part at all?
flow.kid: Count your pairs. Then sort all the pairs by what carries the pull.
flow.think: Could there be a muscle anywhere in any animal with nothing at all to pull it long again?
flow.context: This is the last step of Pair Up. You sort the 12 pairs by what carries the pull between the two partners.

games.title: Joint Detective: which kind of joint did that?
games.context: This is an acting game about the six kinds of moving joint. One player does a small action slowly. The others say which joint did most of the moving, and which kind of joint it is.

printables.title: 18 action cards: the action on the front, the joint and its kind on the back

items.f: Shake your head to say no.
items.b: Pivot joint, at the top of the neck. One bone turns round a peg on the bone below.

items.f: Turn a key in a lock.
items.b: Pivot joint, near the elbow. One forearm bone rolls over the other to turn the palm.

items.f: Bend your arm to scratch your shoulder.
items.b: Hinge joint, the elbow. It bends one way and back.

items.f: Kick a football with a straight swing from the knee.
items.b: Hinge joint, the knee. It bends one way and back.

items.f: Curl one finger to say 'come here'.
items.b: Hinge joints, in the finger. Each one bends one way and back.

items.f: Swing your arm in a full circle, like a bowler.
items.b: Ball and socket joint, the shoulder. A ball turns in a cup.

items.f: Lift your knee and draw a circle in the air with it.
items.b: Ball and socket joint, the hip. A ball turns in a deep cup.

items.f: Touch your thumb to the tip of your little finger.
items.b: Saddle joint, at the base of the thumb. It bends two ways.

items.f: Hold a tumbler with your thumb on one side and fingers on the other.
items.b: Saddle joint, at the base of the thumb. It swings the thumb across the palm.

items.f: Wave goodbye with your hand, keeping your arm still.
items.b: Ellipsoid joint, the wrist. It bends up and down and side to side, but it does not spin.

items.f: Spread your fingers wide apart and close them.
items.b: Ellipsoid joints, the knuckles. They bend two ways.

items.f: Flap your hand up and down as if fanning a fire.
items.b: Ellipsoid joint, the wrist. It bends up and down.

items.f: Press your palm flat on a table and lean on it.
items.b: Gliding joints, between the small wrist bones. Flat surfaces slide a little.

items.f: Stand on a slope so your foot tilts.
items.b: Gliding joints, between the small ankle bones. Flat surfaces slide a little.

items.f: Nod your head to say yes.
items.b: Ellipsoid joint, between the skull and the top neck bone. It rocks forward and back.
The jaw joint. It works as a hinge, and it can also slide forward and sideways.

items.f: Tap the top of your head.
items.b: No movement. The skull bones meet at fixed joints called sutures.

items.f: Twist the lid off a jar.
items.b: Pivot joint near the elbow, helped by the shoulder. The forearm bones roll to turn the hand.

printables.title: A mat with seven spaces
items: Hinge: bends one way and back
Ball and socket: swings in a circle
Pivot: turns round
Saddle: bends two ways, at the thumb
Ellipsoid: bends two ways, does not spin
Gliding: slides a little
Fixed: does not move

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, action side up. Lay out the mat.
On your turn, take the top card. Do not show the back.
Do the action slowly, three times. Say nothing.
The other players each point to a space on the mat. Then they name the joint on the body.
Turn the card over and read the back. Each player who chose the right kind of joint scores 1 point.
Put the card on its space on the mat. The next player takes a turn.
Playing alone, read each card, do the action, and put the card on a space. Then check the back. Count how many you placed correctly.

setup.art: A paper mat with seven labelled spaces on the floor and a pile of cards beside it, action side up.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the 18 cards and the mat. Put the pile action side up.

setup.art: A girl slowly turning an imaginary key while a boy and a parent watch her forearm closely.
setup.caption: 2. Do the action slowly, three times. The others watch which joint moves.

setup.art: Two hands pointing at different spaces on the mat, and the actor turning the card over to read the back.
setup.caption: 3. Each player points to a kind of joint. Turn the card over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 18 cards and the mat. 2. Read the seven spaces of the mat aloud. 3. For each space, find one joint of that kind on your own body.
flow.say: Each space is one kind of joint. Before we play, find one joint of each kind on your own body.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the mat. Read the seven spaces. Find each joint on your body.
flow.context: This is the first step of Joint Detective. You set out the mat of joint kinds and find each kind on your body.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to take a card and do the action slowly. 2. The others point to a space and name the joint. 3. Turn the card over and score.
flow.say: Watch closely. Which joint is doing most of the moving? What shape must the bone ends have to move like that?
flow.kid: Do the action slowly. The others guess the kind of joint. Turn the card to check.

ask.q: How can you tell a pivot from a hinge?
good: A pivot turns round, like a key.
A hinge swings open and shut, like a door.

flow.parent: Most actions use several joints. The card names the one that does most of the moving. If your child names a different joint and can show it moving, give the point.
flow.context: This is the main part of Joint Detective. You watch an action and work out which kind of joint did it.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Look at the mat. 3. Ask which space has the most cards and which has the fewest.
flow.say: Which kind of joint did we use most? Which did we use least? Why might hinges be so common?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which space on the mat has the most cards?
flow.think: A hinge is simple and strong but moves one way only. Where on your body would a hinge be a poor choice?
flow.context: This is the last step of Joint Detective. You count which kinds of joint the actions used most.

experiments.title: The Dough Worm: if a body gets half as wide, how much longer does it get?
experiments.context: In this experiment you roll a lump of chapati dough thinner and thinner, and measure its length each time. Dough keeps its volume when it is squeezed, as the liquid inside an earthworm does. So the dough shows how much longer a worm gets when ring muscles squeeze the body thinner.
experiments.question: An earthworm's ring muscles squeeze a segment thinner, and the segment gets longer. If a roll of dough is squeezed to half its width, how many times as long does it become?
experiments.predict: Guess first. A roll of dough is 4 centimetres wide and 4 centimetres long. You roll it until it is 2 centimetres wide. How long will it be? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The same lump is used from start to finish, and nothing is pinched off or added. The roll is kept the same width all along, and the ends are patted flat before measuring. The width is checked in three places with a card gauge. A second, smaller lump is tested in the same way, to see whether the rule holds at another size.
results_table: How many times the starting length

materials.item: firm chapati dough: about 1 cup of atta mixed with water and a few drops of oil. It must not stick to your hands. Maida dough or modelling clay also works
a clean steel plate, a rolling board or a clean kitchen counter
a piece of card about the size of a postcard, and scissors, for the width gauge

experiments.safety: A grown-up helps with the scissors when cutting the card gauge.

schedule.what: Make the dough and the card gauge. Guess, then roll one lump from 4 centimetres wide to 3 and to 2, measuring the length each time. Repeat with a small lump from 2 centimetres wide to 1.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table. Under it, write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the length of one lump at three widths
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A postcard-sized card with four square notches cut along one edge, labelled 4, 3, 2 and 1 centimetres, beside a ruler and a lump of dough.
setup.caption: 1. Cut four notches in a card: 4, 3, 2 and 1 centimetres wide. This is your width gauge.

setup.art: A short fat roll of dough standing on a steel plate, just fitting the widest notch of the card, with a ruler showing it is 4 centimetres long.
setup.caption: 2. Shape the dough into a roll 4 centimetres wide and 4 centimetres long.
