setup.caption: 3. Roll it evenly until it just fits the 2 centimetre notch all along.

setup.art: A long even roll of dough lying beside a ruler, with its ends patted flat, and a child writing a number in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Pat the ends flat. Measure the length. Write it down.

flow.do: 1. Mix about 1 cup of atta with water and a few drops of oil. 2. Knead until the dough is firm and does not stick. 3. Cut four notches in a card, 4, 3, 2 and 1 centimetres wide.
flow.say: This dough will stand in for an earthworm's body. When you squeeze dough, does the amount of dough change?
flow.kid: Make firm dough that does not stick. Cut four notches in a card.
flow.parent: Sticky dough will not roll evenly, so add a little dry atta until it is firm. Measure each notch with the ruler before cutting. The notch only needs to be as deep as it is wide.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dough Worm. You make firm dough and a card gauge with notches of four widths.

flow.do: 1. Take a lump of dough the size of a large lemon. 2. Shape it into a roll that just fits the 4 centimetre notch. 3. Pinch off or add dough until it is 4 centimetres long. 4. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: This roll is 4 centimetres wide and 4 long. We will roll it to 2 centimetres wide. How long will it be then? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Make a roll 4 centimetres wide and 4 long. Guess its length at 2 centimetres wide. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think it will be that long?
good: Half as wide, so twice as long: 8 centimetres.
It gets thinner all round, so maybe more than twice.
The dough has to go somewhere.

flow.parent: Most children, and most adults, say 8 centimetres. Do not correct the guess. Write it in the table with the reason. Also ask for a guess at 3 centimetres wide.
flow.context: This is the second step of the Dough Worm. You make the starting roll and guess how long it will be at half the width.

flow.do: 1. Roll the dough under flat palms until it just fits the 3 centimetre notch all along. 2. Pat both ends flat with the ruler. 3. Measure the length and write it down. 4. Roll on to the 2 centimetre notch and measure again.
flow.say: Keep it even all along. Check the width at both ends and in the middle. Now measure the length.
flow.kid: Roll it to 3 centimetres wide. Measure the length. Then roll it to 2 and measure again.
flow.parent: At 3 centimetres wide the roll is usually close to 7 centimetres long. At 2 centimetres wide it is usually between 14 and 18. The ends of a roll go thin, so push them in and pat them flat before measuring. If the roll cracks, knead in two drops of water and start again from 4 centimetres.

check.q: In the Dough Worm, why must you never pinch off any dough once you start rolling?
options: The amount of dough must stay the same
The dough would dry out
Small bits are hard to roll
check.why: The test asks what happens to length when width changes and nothing else does. If dough were removed, the roll would be shorter for a different reason. If you chose 'dry out', notice that drying is a separate problem and does not change the question being tested.

flow.context: In this step of the Dough Worm, you roll the dough to 3 and then 2 centimetres wide and measure its length each time.

flow.do: 1. Take a small lump, the size of a marble or a little bigger. 2. Shape it to fit the 2 centimetre notch, 4 centimetres long. 3. Ask for a new guess. 4. Roll it to fit the 1 centimetre notch and measure.
flow.say: This small roll is 2 centimetres wide and 4 long. We will roll it to 1 centimetre wide. Now what do you guess, and why?
flow.kid: Make a small roll 2 centimetres wide and 4 long. Guess again. Roll it to 1 centimetre wide. Measure.
flow.parent: This is the same halving at a smaller size. Many children now guess 16, using the pattern from the first lump. A thin roll breaks easily. Roll gently with your fingers spread, and work on a counter if the plate is too small.
flow.context: In this step of the Dough Worm, you test a smaller lump to see whether the same rule holds at another size.

flow.do: 1. For each row, divide the measured length by the starting length of 4. 2. Write the answer in the last column. 3. Look down the column together.
flow.say: Divide each length by 4. When the width was halved, about how many times as long did the roll become? Was it the same for both lumps?
flow.kid: Divide each length by 4. What happened each time the width was halved?
flow.parent: Answers between 3 and a half and 4 and a half times are good results. Hand rolling is never perfectly even.
flow.context: In this step of the Dough Worm, you work out how many times as long the roll became each time.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say what they thought would happen, what they saw, and why they think it happened. 2. Cut the 2 centimetre roll across and look at the cut face. 3. After they have answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why. Now look at the cut end. How does it compare with the cut end of the fat roll?
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened.

ask.q: Why four times as long, and not twice?
good: It got thinner from side to side and from top to bottom at once.
The cut end is a much smaller circle, so the dough needs more length.
It is half in two directions.

ask.q: What does this tell you about an earthworm's ring muscles?
good: A small squeeze makes the worm a lot longer.
The worm gets longer because the liquid cannot be squashed smaller.

flow.parent: The reason: the roll is round, so it gets narrower from side to side and from top to bottom at once. The cut face of the 2 centimetre roll is a circle with a quarter of the area of the 4 centimetre one. The same dough behind a face a quarter of the size needs four times the length. An earthworm's liquid keeps its volume in the same way, and so does the muscle of a tongue. A small squeeze across gives a large reach along. If the dough is clean, it can go into the day's chapatis.
flow.think: To stick your tongue out twice as far, would it have to become half as wide, or less narrow than that?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Dough Worm. You say what you found and why halving the width gave about four times the length.

experiments.title: The Finger Lift: which finger can lift highest all alone?
experiments.context: In this experiment you lay your hand flat on a table and lift one finger at a time, while the others stay down. You measure how high each fingertip goes. It shows that the muscles and tendons of your fingers are not five separate sets.
experiments.question: With the other fingers held flat on the table, does every finger lift to the same height? If not, which lifts least?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Your hand lies flat, and you lift one finger while the other four stay down. Put the five fingers in order, from the one that will lift highest to the one that will lift least. Why do you think so? Write your order and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: The palm and the other four fingertips stay flat on the table every time. Each finger is lifted as high as it will go without pain, and held for a count of three. The height is measured from the table to the underside of the fingertip, with the same ruler held upright. Each finger is measured twice.

materials.item: a ruler marked in centimetres and millimetres
a helper to hold the ruler and read it

schedule.what: Guess the order. Measure the lift of each finger twice with the others held flat. Measure the ring finger again with its neighbours free. Draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the results table and draw a bar chart of the five averages. Under it, write what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: how high each fingertip lifted, with the others flat
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A child's hand lying flat on a table, palm down, with all five fingertips touching the wood.
setup.caption: 1. Lay one hand flat on the table, palm down, fingers a little apart.

setup.art: The same hand with only the index finger lifted high, and a helper's hand holding a ruler upright beside the fingertip.
setup.caption: 2. Lift one finger as high as it goes. The other four stay down. A helper measures the height.

setup.art: The same hand with the ring finger lifted only a little way, the ruler beside it, and the child looking surprised.
setup.caption: 3. Do this for every finger, twice. Write each height in the table.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to lay one hand flat on the table. 2. Ask them to guess the order of the fingers, from highest lift to least. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write both down.
flow.say: You will lift one finger while the other four stay flat. Which will go highest? Which will go least? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lay your hand flat. Guess which finger will lift highest and which least. Say why.

ask.q: Why do you think that finger will lift least?
good: The little finger is the smallest, so it is weakest.
The ring finger always feels stuck.
They should all be the same, because each finger has its own muscle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children pick the little finger as the lowest, because it is the smallest.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Finger Lift. You guess which finger can lift highest while the others stay flat.

flow.do: 1. Keep the palm and four fingertips on the table. 2. Lift the thumb as high as it goes and hold for a count of three. 3. The helper measures from the table to the underside of the fingertip. 4. Repeat for each finger, then do the whole hand a second time.
flow.say: Lift only this finger. Keep the others down. Hold it there while I measure. Did any other finger want to rise?
flow.kid: Lift one finger. Keep the others flat. Hold it for a count of three. Do every finger twice.
flow.parent: Stop at the first feeling of stretch. Nobody should force a finger. If a neighbouring finger lifts off the table, start that try again. The ring finger usually lifts least, often only 1 to 2 centimetres. Hands differ, so write what you really find.

check.q: In the Finger Lift, why is each finger measured twice?
options: One try can be a fluke
The second try is always higher
To tire the finger out
check.why: A single measurement can be off because the hand shifted or the ruler was read badly. Two tries and an average give a fairer number. If you chose 'always higher', look at your own table to see whether that is true.

flow.context: In this step of the Finger Lift, you measure how high each finger lifts while the other four stay flat on the table.

flow.do: 1. Lay the hand flat again. 2. Lift the ring finger, and this time let the middle and little fingers rise with it if they want to. 3. Measure the ring fingertip. 4. Write it in the last column.
flow.say: Now let the neighbours come up too, if they want to. How high does the ring finger go this time? What does that tell you?
flow.kid: Lift your ring finger again. This time let its neighbours rise too. Measure it.
flow.parent: With its neighbours free, the ring finger usually goes much higher. This points to a link between the fingers and not to a weak finger.
flow.context: In this step of the Finger Lift, you measure the ring finger again while its neighbours are free to rise with it.

flow.do: 1. Work out the average of the two tries for each finger. 2. Draw a bar chart of the five averages. 3. Ask your child to say what they thought, what they saw and why. 4. After they have answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Look at your chart. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
flow.kid: Find each average. Draw five bars. Say what you guessed, what you saw and why.

ask.q: The ring finger went higher when its neighbours were free. What does that suggest?
good: The ring finger is tied to its neighbours.
Its muscle is strong enough, but something holds it back.
The fingers share something.

ask.q: Where are the muscles that lift your fingers?
good: In the forearm.
Not in the fingers. I can see the cords on the back of my hand.

flow.parent: The reason: the muscles that straighten the fingers are in the forearm, and long tendons carry their pull over the back of the hand. Small bands join the tendons of the middle, ring and little fingers to each other. So when the neighbours are held down, the ring finger's tendon is held down too. The index finger and the little finger each have an extra straightening muscle of their own, and the ring finger has none. Scientists who measured this found that these links are a main cause. The way the brain controls the forearm muscles adds to it.
flow.think: A veena player or a typist trains for years. Do you think practice can change these links, or only the control?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Finger Lift. You chart the heights and say why one finger lifts less than the others.

activities.title: The Tongue Puzzle: what pushes a tongue out?
activities.context: This is a short activity to do before any explaining. Muscles can only pull, yet a tongue comes forward out of the mouth. You watch your own tongue in a mirror and draw what you think is happening inside it.
activities.record: Write the two widths of your tongue. Draw what you think is inside a tongue that makes it go out. Keep the drawing, and look at it again at the end of the unit.

setup.art: A child bending her elbow and feeling the front of her upper arm with her other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Bend your arm and feel the muscle pull. A muscle can only pull.

setup.art: A child looking in a mirror with her tongue resting wide and flat on her lower lip, a ruler held just below it.
setup.caption: 2. Rest your tongue on your lip. Look at how wide and thick it is.

setup.art: The same child with her tongue stretched far out and pointed, the ruler below it, and a notebook open beside the mirror.
setup.caption: 3. Stick it out as far as you can. Look again. Draw what you think is inside.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to bend an elbow and feel the upper arm. 2. Say that every muscle works by pulling. 3. Ask what moves the tongue forward.
flow.say: Feel that muscle pull your arm up. Every muscle only pulls. So what moves your tongue forward, out of your mouth? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Bend your arm. Feel the muscle pull. Now, what moves your tongue forward? Guess, and say why.

good: A muscle behind it pushes.
Something pulls it from the front.
It stretches somehow.

flow.parent: Do not correct any guess. 'A muscle pushes it' is the most common answer, and the unit will come back to it.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tongue Puzzle. You guess how a tongue can come forward when muscles can only pull.

flow.do: 1. In front of a mirror, your child rests the tongue wide and flat on the lower lip. 2. Hold a ruler just below it and read the width. 3. Your child sticks the tongue out as far as it goes. 4. Read the width again.
flow.say: Look at your tongue resting. How wide is it? How thick? Now stick it right out. What has changed, apart from the length?
flow.kid: Rest your tongue on your lip. Measure how wide it is. Stick it right out. Measure again.
flow.parent: Hold the ruler near the tongue without touching it. A resting tongue is often 4 to 5 centimetres wide. Stuck out and pointed, it is usually about 1 centimetre narrower, and thinner too. Write what you really see.
flow.context: In this step of the Tongue Puzzle, you compare the width of your tongue when it rests and when it is stuck out.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to draw a tongue and what might be inside it. 2. Ask them to show with arrows what pulls where. 3. Keep the drawing for the end of the unit.
flow.say: Draw what you think is inside your tongue. Use arrows to show what pulls. We will look at this drawing again later.
flow.kid: Draw your tongue and what is inside it. Add arrows for the pulls. Keep the drawing.
flow.think: Your tongue got narrower as it got longer. Could those two changes be connected?
flow.context: This is the last step of the Tongue Puzzle. You draw what you think happens inside a tongue when it goes out.

activities.title: Who Is Working Now? Three pairs and one surprise
activities.context: In this activity you feel which muscle of a pair is firm during a movement. You try the knee and the ankle. Then you lower a full tumbler slowly and find out which muscle is working, which is not the one most people expect.

materials.item: a steel tumbler full of water

activities.record: Draw a table with three rows: knee, ankle, elbow. For each, write which muscle bends the joint and which straightens it. Under it, write what you found when you lowered the tumbler.

setup.art: A child sitting on a chair with one hand on the front of her thigh and one under it, straightening her knee.
setup.caption: 1. Sit. Put one hand on top of your thigh and one under it. Straighten your knee, then pull your heel back.

setup.art: A child standing on tiptoe with a hand on her calf, and then standing on her heels with toes lifted and a hand on her shin.
setup.caption: 2. Stand. Rise on your toes, then lift your toes. Feel the calf and the shin.

setup.art: A child slowly lowering a full steel tumbler from her shoulder to a table while a parent's fingers rest on the front and back of her upper arm.
setup.caption: 3. Lower a full tumbler slowly. A helper feels the front and back of your upper arm.

flow.do: 1. Your child sits on a chair with one hand on top of the thigh and one under it. 2. They straighten the knee and hold it. 3. They pull the heel back hard against the chair leg. 4. Ask which hand felt a firm muscle each time.
flow.say: Straighten your knee. Which hand feels the muscle go firm? Now pull your heel back against the chair. Which hand feels it now?
flow.kid: Sit down. Straighten your knee. Then pull your heel back. Which side of your thigh goes firm?
flow.parent: The front of the thigh goes firm to straighten the knee. The back of the thigh goes firm to bend it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Who Is Working Now. You find the pair of muscles that straighten and bend the knee.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands and holds the table for balance. 2. They rise on their toes and feel the calf. 3. They stand on their heels with toes lifted and feel the front of the shin.
flow.say: Rise on your toes and feel your calf. Now lift your toes and feel beside your shin bone. Which muscle did which job?
flow.kid: Rise on your toes. Feel your calf. Now lift your toes. Feel your shin.
flow.context: In this step of Who Is Working Now, you find the pair of muscles that point the foot down and lift it up.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds a full tumbler at the shoulder, elbow bent. 2. Ask which muscle will be working while the arm lowers, and why. 3. They lower the tumbler to the table over a slow count of five. 4. You feel the front and the back of their upper arm as it lowers.
flow.say: Your elbow will straighten as the tumbler goes down. Which muscle will be working, the front one or the back one? Why? Now lower it slowly.
flow.kid: Hold a full tumbler at your shoulder. Guess which arm muscle will work. Lower it slowly.

ask.q: Your elbow was straightening. Why was the front muscle firm and not the back one?
good: The weight was pulling my arm down by itself.
The front muscle was holding it back so it did not drop.
Gravity did the straightening.

flow.parent: Most people guess the triceps, because the elbow is straightening. It is the biceps that is firm. Gravity is straightening the arm, and the biceps is letting it down a little at a time. So here gravity is the partner. Let your child say what they felt before you say this.

check.q: You lower a heavy bag slowly to the floor, and your elbow straightens. Which muscle is working hardest?
options: The biceps, letting the arm down
The triceps, pushing the arm down
Neither, because the arm is going down
check.why: The weight of the bag straightens the elbow. The biceps works to slow it. If you chose the triceps, remember that a muscle cannot push, and that the bag needs no help to go down.

flow.context: In this step of Who Is Working Now, you lower a full tumbler slowly and feel which upper-arm muscle is firm.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to make one arm as stiff as a stick, half bent. 2. Feel the front and the back of the upper arm. 3. Ask what both muscles are doing.
flow.say: Make your arm stiff, half bent, so I cannot move it. Feel the front and the back. What are the two partners doing now?
flow.kid: Make your arm stiff. Feel the front and the back. What are both muscles doing?
flow.think: When you write with a pencil, do the partners in your hand take turns, or do both pull at once?
flow.context: This is the last step of Who Is Working Now. You feel both muscles of a pair pulling at once to hold a joint stiff.

activities.title: Joint Hunt: find six kinds of joint on your own body
activities.context: In this activity you move one joint at a time and work out how it is built from the way it moves. There are six kinds of moving joint. You find each kind on your body and match it to something in your home that moves in the same way.

materials.item: a door, a key in a lock, and a spoon with a lemon or an egg-shaped pebble

activities.record: Draw a table with three columns: the kind of joint, where I found it on my body, and something at home that moves in the same way. Fill in six rows.

setup.art: A child holding her upper arm still with one hand while bending and straightening the elbow, beside an open door.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the bone above a joint still. Move only that joint. Which ways can it go?

setup.art: A child turning her palm up and down with her elbow tucked in, beside a hand turning a key in a lock.
setup.caption: 2. Match the movement to something at home: a door, a key, a ball in a cup.

setup.art: A notebook table with six rows and three columns, half filled in a child's handwriting.
setup.caption: 3. Write each joint in your table, with its kind and its match at home.

flow.do: 1. Open and shut a door together. 2. Turn a key in a lock. 3. Roll a lemon in a spoon. 4. Ask how each one moves and what stops it from moving other ways.
flow.say: A door swings one way and back. A key turns round. The lemon in the spoon tilts two ways. What shape lets each one move like that?
flow.kid: Swing a door. Turn a key. Tilt a lemon in a spoon. How does each one move?
flow.context: This is the first step of Joint Hunt. You look at three things at home that move in three different ways.

flow.do: 1. Your child holds the upper arm still and moves only the elbow. 2. They name the ways it can move. 3. Repeat for the shoulder, the wrist, the base of the thumb, the neck and a finger. 4. For each, they guess the kind of joint and write it down.
flow.say: Hold the bone above the joint still. Move only the joint. Does it swing one way, two ways, in a circle, or turn round?
flow.kid: Hold still above the joint. Move only the joint. How many ways does it go? Write it down.

ask.q: Your elbow bends, and your palm can also turn up and down. Is that one joint or two?
good: Two. The hinge bends the arm.
A different joint lets one forearm bone roll over the other.

flow.parent: Elbow and finger joints are hinges. The shoulder is a ball and socket. Turning the palm and turning the head use pivots. The base of the thumb is a saddle. The wrist is an ellipsoid joint, which tilts two ways but does not spin. When the hand seems to spin, the turning is in the forearm.
flow.context: In this step of Joint Hunt, you test six joints one at a time and decide which kind each one is.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to press between the small bones on the back of the wrist while moving the hand. 2. Explain that these flat joints slide a little. 3. Ask them to feel the top of the head for any movement. 4. Complete the table.
flow.say: Press here on your wrist and move your hand. These small bones slide a little on each other. Now feel your skull. Does anything move there?
flow.kid: Press on your wrist and move your hand. Then feel your skull. Finish your table.

check.q: A joint can bend up and down and side to side, but it cannot spin. Which kind is it?
options: Ellipsoid, like the wrist
Hinge, like the elbow
Ball and socket, like the hip
check.why: An oval knob in an oval cup can tilt two ways, but an oval cannot spin in an oval hole. A hinge goes one way only. A ball and socket can also spin, as when you roll your whole arm at the shoulder.

flow.context: This is the last step of Joint Hunt. You find gliding joints in the wrist and fixed joints in the skull.

activities.title: The Water Balloon Worm: feel a skeleton made of water
activities.context: In this activity a balloon full of water stands in for one segment of an earthworm. One person's hands are the ring muscles and another person's hands are the lengthwise muscles. You feel how each squeeze stretches the other pair of hands.

materials.item: a tap, and a tray or a bathroom floor to work over

activities.safety: A balloon can burst, so work over a tray or in the bathroom. Keep balloons and bits of burst balloon away from children under five, who can choke on them.
activities.record: Write the length of the balloon at rest, when squeezed round the middle, and when pressed from the ends. Draw the balloon three times with arrows for the squeezes.

setup.art: A grown-up holding the neck of a balloon over a tap as it fills with water to the size of a small mango.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up fills a balloon with water to the size of a small mango and ties it.

setup.art: A child's two hands making a ring round the middle of a water balloon on a tray, with the ends bulging out and a ruler beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Squeeze round the middle. Measure the length.

setup.art: A parent's palms pressing on the two ends of the balloon while the child's ring of hands is pushed wider.
setup.caption: 3. A helper presses the two ends together. Feel your ring of hands pushed apart.

flow.do: 1. Stretch the neck of a balloon over a tap. 2. Fill it slowly to the size of a small mango. 3. Squeeze out any air and tie the neck. 4. Lay it on a tray and measure its length.
flow.say: This balloon is one segment of an earthworm: a bag of liquid. If I squeeze round its middle, what will happen to its length? Why?
flow.kid: A grown-up fills and ties the balloon. Measure it. Guess what a squeeze round the middle will do.
flow.parent: About one tumbler of water is enough. A balloon filled too tight bursts easily. Dry the outside so that it is easy to hold.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Water Balloon Worm. A grown-up fills a balloon with water and you guess what a squeeze will do.

flow.do: 1. Your child makes a ring round the middle of the balloon with both hands. 2. They squeeze gently. 3. You measure the length. 4. They let go, and you measure again.
flow.say: You are the ring muscles. Squeeze gently round the middle. What happened to the length? Where did the water go?
flow.kid: Make a ring with your hands round the middle. Squeeze gently. What happens to the length?
flow.parent: The balloon gets clearly longer, often by 2 to 4 centimetres. Squeeze gently. A hard squeeze can burst it.
flow.context: In this step of the Water Balloon Worm, your hands act as ring muscles and you measure how the balloon lengthens.

flow.do: 1. Your child keeps the ring of hands on, without squeezing. 2. You press the two ends of the balloon towards each other with flat palms. 3. Ask what their hands feel. 4. Swap roles and repeat.
flow.say: Now I am the lengthwise muscles. I press the ends together. What do your hands feel? Now you squeeze, and I will feel my palms.
flow.kid: Keep your hands round the middle. A helper presses the ends together. What do your hands feel?

ask.q: Your hands never touched mine. How did my push reach your hands?
good: Through the water.
The water cannot be squashed smaller, so it pushed outwards on my hands.

flow.context: In this step of the Water Balloon Worm, one person's squeeze pushes the other person's hands apart through the water.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child what the water did for the two pairs of hands. 2. Ask what does that job in an arm. 3. After they have answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Each pair of hands was stretched by the other. What carried the push between them? What carries the pull between your biceps and your triceps?
flow.kid: Each pair of hands stretched the other. What carried the push? What does that in your arm?
flow.parent: The water keeps its volume, so a squeeze one way comes out as a push another way. That is how an earthworm's ring muscles stretch the lengthwise muscles, and the lengthwise muscles stretch the ring muscles. The liquid does for the worm what the forearm bone does for your biceps and triceps. Pour the water on a plant when you finish.

check.q: An earthworm's circular muscles contract. What happens to that segment?
options: It gets thinner and longer
It gets shorter and fatter
It gets smaller all over
check.why: The liquid inside cannot be squeezed into less space. A segment that is made thinner must get longer. If you chose 'smaller all over', think of the balloon: the water had to go somewhere.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Water Balloon Worm. You compare the water in the balloon with the bone in your arm.

activities.title: Armour Up Close: find the joints in an exoskeleton
activities.context: In this activity you look closely at a real exoskeleton. If your family cooks prawns or crab, use a shell from the kitchen. If not, use the shed skin of a cicada, or watch a live ant or a cockroach through a hand lens.

materials.item: the shell of a cooked prawn or a crab leg from the kitchen, or a shed insect skin, or a live ant on a plate
a hand lens, or a phone camera held close
a toothpick, a white plate and a notebook

activities.safety: Do not handle prawn or crab if anyone at the table is allergic to shellfish. Wash your hands with soap afterwards.
activities.record: Draw one leg or one part of the tail. Mark the hard tubes or plates in one colour and the soft joints in another. Write where you think the muscles were.

setup.art: A prawn shell and a crab leg on a white plate beside a hand lens and a toothpick.
setup.caption: 1. Put the shell on a white plate. Look at it through a hand lens.

setup.art: A close view of a prawn's tail bent and straightened by two fingers, with the thin clear skin between the hard plates showing.
setup.caption: 2. Bend it gently. Find where it bends and where it cannot.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a jointed leg with hard parts shaded and soft joints left white.
setup.caption: 3. Draw it. Colour the hard parts and the soft joints differently.

flow.do: 1. Put the shell or insect skin on a white plate. 2. Ask your child to guess where it can bend. 3. Ask for a reason.
flow.say: This skeleton was on the outside. Where do you think it can bend? Why there?
flow.kid: Look at the shell. Guess where it can bend. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Armour Up Close. You guess where a hard outer skeleton is able to bend.

flow.do: 1. Bend the tail or the leg gently in several places. 2. With the lens, look at the skin between two hard parts. 3. Press a hard part and a joint with the toothpick. 4. Look inside a broken crab leg, if you have one.
flow.say: Bend it gently. Is the bending spread out, or only in certain places? What is different about the shell at those places?
flow.kid: Bend it gently. Look at where it bends with the lens. Press the hard part and the joint.

ask.q: The shell is on the outside. So where were the muscles?
good: Inside the tubes.
The prawn meat we eat is the muscle that bent the tail.

flow.parent: The hard plates do not bend. Between them the covering is thin, clear and soft. The meat of a prawn's tail is the large muscle that curls the tail. In a crab's claw you may find a flat white blade. The claw's closing muscle was fixed to it. With a live ant, do not touch them. Watch where the legs bend, and let them go afterwards.
flow.context: In this step of Armour Up Close, you find the soft joints between the hard parts of an exoskeleton.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws one leg or part of the tail. 2. They colour hard parts and soft joints differently. 3. They draw where two muscles could sit inside one tube.
flow.say: Draw it. Then draw two muscles inside one tube, one to bend the next joint and one to straighten it.
flow.kid: Draw the leg. Colour hard parts and soft joints. Draw two muscles inside one tube.
flow.think: This animal could not grow without throwing the whole shell away. What would that be like for you?
flow.context: This is the last step of Armour Up Close. You draw an exoskeleton and where its pair of muscles would be.

activities.title: Droop and Rise: a water skeleton in a plant
activities.context: In this activity you let a stalk of fresh coriander droop, and then stand it in water and watch it rise. A plant has no bones and no muscles. Soft stalks and leaves are held up by water pressing outward inside every cell.

materials.item: fresh coriander, palak or methi with soft stalks

activities.record: Draw the two stalks at the start, after three hours and after standing in water. Write what you think changed inside the stalk.

schedule.what: Stand two stalks in water and leave two on a dry plate. Look after three hours. Then stand the drooping stalks in water and look again one to three hours later.

setup.art: Two coriander stalks standing in a steel tumbler of water and two more lying on a dry plate on a kitchen counter.
setup.caption: 1. Stand two stalks in water. Leave two on a dry plate.

setup.art: The same scene three hours later, with the stalks on the plate limp and curled and the ones in water upright.
setup.caption: 2. After three hours, hold each stalk by its end. Which ones droop?

setup.art: The limp stalks now standing in the tumbler with freshly cut ends, beginning to straighten.
setup.caption: 3. Snip the ends of the drooping stalks. Stand them in water. Look again later.

flow.do: 1. Choose four fresh stalks of the same size. 2. Stand two in a tumbler of water. 3. Lay two on a dry plate, away from the sun. 4. Ask what will happen to each pair, and why.
flow.say: Two stalks get water and two get none. What will each pair look like after three hours? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Stand two stalks in water. Leave two on a plate. Guess what will happen. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Droop and Rise. You set up two stalks with water and two without, and guess what will happen.

flow.do: 1. Hold each stalk by its cut end, pointing sideways. 2. Compare how far the tips hang down. 3. Snip a little off the ends of the drooping stalks. 4. Stand them in the water.
flow.say: Hold each one out sideways. Which ones hold themselves up? What do you think the limp ones have lost?
flow.kid: Hold each stalk out sideways. Which ones droop? Snip the ends and stand them in water.
flow.parent: On a hot dry day the stalks droop within an hour. On a humid day it can take longer than three hours. Snipping the end opens fresh tubes for the water to enter.
flow.context: In this step of Droop and Rise, you compare the stalks after three hours and put the limp ones in water.

flow.do: 1. Look at the stalks that were limp. 2. Hold them out sideways again. 3. Ask your child what they thought, what they saw and why. 4. After they have answered, read the note below aloud.
flow.say: Hold them out again. What has changed? Nothing was added but water. So what was holding the stalk up?
flow.kid: Look at the limp stalks now. Hold them out. What held them up? Say why you think so.

ask.q: The plant has no bones. What holds up a soft stalk?
good: Water inside it.
The cells are full of water and press outward.
It is like the water balloon.

flow.parent: Most soft stalks rise again within one to three hours. A stalk that has dried too far may not recover. If so, say that some cells were damaged. The reason: each plant cell is a small box with a firm wall. When it is full of water, the water presses on the wall and the cell is stiff. Many stiff cells hold the stalk up. This is a water skeleton, like the earthworm's, but in a being with no muscles.

check.q: A wilted plant stands up again after watering. What changed inside the stalk?
options: The cells filled with water and went stiff
The plant grew new hard fibres
The water made the stalk heavier
check.why: Water refills each cell and presses on its wall, so the cell is firm again. New fibres could not grow in an hour or two. Extra weight alone would make a stalk droop more, not less.

flow.context: This is the last step of Droop and Rise. You see whether water alone can make a limp stalk firm again.

projects.title: The Bend Survey: do young joints bend further than old ones?
projects.context: In this three-day project you measure how far two joints bend in people of different ages. Ligaments and other tissues round a joint set how far it can go. You find out whether that changes with age in the people you know.

materials.item: a protractor from a geometry box
8 or more family members, neighbours or friends of different ages who agree to be measured

projects.safety: Nobody pushes or pulls another person's joint. Each person moves their own joint and stops at the first feeling of stretch. Leave out anyone with a painful or injured wrist or back.

schedule.what: Write the question and your guess. Practise the two measurements on yourself and one other person.
Measure at least 8 people of different ages. Write their age group, not their name.
Draw a bar chart for each measurement. Write a short report, with one thing the survey cannot show.

projects.record: A table of results, two bar charts and a short report. The report ends with one sentence on what the survey cannot show.

setup.art: A forearm resting flat on a table with the hand lifted back at the wrist, and a protractor held upright beside the wrist to read the angle.
setup.caption: 1. Wrist test: rest the forearm on a table. Lift the hand back. Read the angle with a protractor.

setup.art: A person sitting on the floor with legs straight and feet flat against a wall, reaching forward, with a ruler measuring from fingertips to the wall.
setup.caption: 2. Reach test: sit with feet against a wall. Reach forward. Measure from the fingertips to the wall.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of age groups and two columns of numbers, and a child drawing bars beneath it.
setup.caption: 3. Measure 8 people. Chart the results by age group.

flow.do: 1. Day 1. Write the question: do young joints bend further than old ones? 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Practise the wrist test and the reach test on yourself and on one other person. 4. Draw a table with columns for age group, wrist angle and reach distance.
flow.say: Who do you think will bend further, children or grandparents? Why do you think so? Let us practise the two tests first.
flow.kid: Write your question and your guess. Say why. Practise both tests on yourself.

ask.q: Why do we measure every person in exactly the same way?
good: So the only difference is the person.
Otherwise we could not compare the numbers.

flow.parent: Wrist test: the forearm lies flat on a table, palm down, with the hand over the edge. The person lifts the hand back as far as it goes. Hold the protractor upright with its centre at the wrist and read the angle between the hand and the table. Reach test: the person sits with legs straight and feet flat against a wall, reaches forward, and you measure the gap from fingertips to the wall. If the fingers reach the wall, write 0.
flow.context: This is day 1 of the Bend Survey. You write a guess and practise two ways of measuring how far a joint bends.

flow.do: 1. Day 2. Measure at least 8 people. 2. Include at least 2 children, 2 adults under 40 and 2 people over 55, if you can. 3. Write each person's age group and two numbers. 4. Do not write names.
flow.say: Ask each person to move gently and stop at the first stretch. Measure everyone the same way. Write the age group, not the name.
flow.kid: Measure 8 people in the same way. Write each age group and two numbers. No names.
flow.parent: Thank each person. Never say that a number is good or bad. People who dance, swim or do yoga often bend further than others of their age.
flow.context: This is day 2 of the Bend Survey. You measure the wrist angle and the reach of at least eight people.

flow.do: 1. Day 3. Work out the average wrist angle for each age group. 2. Do the same for the reach. 3. Draw a bar chart for each. 4. Write what you found, and one thing the survey cannot show.
flow.say: What do the charts show? Does it match your guess? Was anyone a surprise? What can a survey of 8 people not tell us?
flow.kid: Find the average for each age group. Draw two bar charts. Write what you found.

ask.q: What can this survey not show?
good: Eight people are too few to speak for everyone.
We do not know if a person bent less when young.
Exercise might matter more than age.

flow.parent: In large studies, joints do tend to bend a little less with age, as ligaments and other tissues stiffen. In a survey of 8 people the pattern may not show, and one supple grandparent can reverse it. That is a real finding about small surveys. Write what you found.
flow.context: This is day 3 of the Bend Survey. You chart your results and say what a small survey can and cannot show.

challenges.title: Build a Crab Claw: open and close it with threads that only pull
challenges.context: A crab's claw is opened and closed by two muscles inside the shell, and each can only pull. This is a design challenge. You build a card claw worked by two threads that run inside a tube.
challenges.problem: Build a claw from card with one fixed finger and one moving finger. Pulling one thread must close the claw, and pulling the other must open it. Both threads must run inside the arm tube and come out at the far end.
constraints: You may only pull on the threads. No pushing the finger with your hand.
Both threads run inside the tube, as muscles run inside a shell.
The claw must open and close ten times without coming apart.
It must pick up a crumpled ball of paper.
materials: thin card, such as an old notebook cover or a biscuit packet
a crumpled ball of paper to pick up
general: Roll card into a tube for the arm. Cut two fingers from card. Tape one finger firmly to the tube so that it cannot move.
Join the moving finger to the tube with a hinge of tape, so that it swings towards the fixed finger and away.
Tie one thread to the moving finger on the inner side of the hinge and one on the outer side. Pass both down the tube. One closes and one opens.
creative: Replace the opening thread with a rubber band on the outside of the hinge. Then one thread closes the claw, and the band opens it, as a springy band opens a clam.
Fix the closing thread a little further from the hinge and see whether the grip gets stronger.
Put a small balloon inside the joint and blow through a straw to open the claw, as a spider straightens a leg with liquid pressure.
challenges.your_turn: Change one thing about your claw so that it grips harder or opens wider. Say what you changed and why you expected it to work. Test it ten times and say what happened.

setup.art: A card tube with one card finger taped firmly to its end and a second finger joined by a tape hinge, lying on a table with thread and scissors.
setup.caption: 1. Make a tube arm. Tape on one fixed finger. Hinge on one moving finger.

setup.art: A close view of the hinge with one thread tied to the inner side of the moving finger and one to the outer side, both running into the tube.
setup.caption: 2. Tie one thread each side of the hinge. Pass both down inside the tube.

setup.art: A child holding the tube in one hand and pulling one of two threads at its far end, as the claw closes on a ball of paper.
setup.caption: 3. Pull one thread to close and the other to open. Pick up a paper ball.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem and the rules together. 2. Ask your child where each thread should be tied, and why. 3. Ask them to sketch the claw before cutting anything.
flow.say: One thread must close the claw and one must open it. Where will you tie each one? Why there? Draw your plan first.
flow.kid: Read the problem. Decide where each thread goes. Say why. Draw your plan.

ask.q: Why does the claw need two threads?
good: A thread can only pull, like a muscle.
One thread cannot undo its own pull.

flow.parent: Let your child place the threads by their own reasoning, even if the first try fails. A thread tied on the hinge itself moves nothing, and finding that out is useful.
flow.context: This is the first step of Build a Crab Claw. You plan where two pulling threads must be tied to open and close a claw.

flow.do: 1. Roll a tube about 15 centimetres long and 3 wide, and tape it. 2. Cut two fingers about 8 centimetres long. 3. Tape one to the tube firmly, and hinge the other with tape. 4. Make two small holes in the moving finger, one each side of the hinge. 5. Tie the threads and pass them down the tube.
flow.say: Build it from your plan. Pull one thread, then the other. Does each do its job? If not, what will you change?
flow.kid: Build your claw. Tie the two threads. Pull each one. Change what does not work.
flow.parent: A grown-up makes the holes with a pencil point over an eraser. If a thread does nothing, it is tied too close to the hinge. Moving the knot 1 centimetre further from the hinge usually fixes it.

check.q: In Build a Crab Claw, the closing thread is tied exactly on the hinge. What happens when you pull it?
options: Nothing moves
The claw closes fast
The claw opens
check.why: A pull turns a finger only if it is applied away from the hinge. On the hinge itself there is nothing to swing. If you chose 'closes fast', try it on your model and see.

flow.context: In this step of Build a Crab Claw, you build the claw and test whether each thread does its job.

flow.do: 1. Open and close the claw ten times. 2. Try to pick up the ball of paper. 3. Change one thing to improve it, and test again. 4. Ask which thread works like which muscle.
flow.say: Test it ten times. Now change one thing to make it grip harder. What did you change, and what happened?
flow.kid: Open and close it ten times. Pick up the paper ball. Change one thing and test again.
flow.think: A real crab's closing muscle is far bigger than the opening muscle. Why might that be?
flow.context: This is the last step of Build a Crab Claw. You test your claw, improve one thing and compare it with a real claw.

worksheets.title: Pairs, joints and three kinds of skeleton (core)

items.p: What can a muscle do?
items.why: A muscle works by getting shorter, and a thing that gets shorter pulls. The threads inside it have no way to push apart.

items.p: Which two muscles are the antagonistic pair of the elbow?
items.why: The biceps bends the elbow and the triceps straightens it. A tendon is a cord, not a muscle.

items.p: A muscle that bends a joint is called a ____.
items.why: A flexor bends a joint. An extensor straightens it.

items.p: The slippery liquid inside a moving joint is called ____ fluid.
items.why: Synovial fluid lets the cartilage surfaces slide, and it carries food to the cartilage.

items.p: Match each joint to its kind.
pairs: Top of the neck, turning the head
items.why: The shape of the bone ends sets the movement. A hinge swings one way, a ball turns in a cup, a pivot turns round, and a saddle bends two ways.

items.p: A tendon joins a bone to another bone.
items.why: False. A tendon joins a muscle to a bone. A ligament joins a bone to a bone.

items.p: The muscles of a crab are inside the skeleton.
items.why: True. A crab has an exoskeleton, which is a skeleton on the outside. The muscles pull from inside the hard tubes.

items.p: How does an animal with an exoskeleton grow?
opts: By adding rings to the shell
items.why: A hard exoskeleton cannot stretch. The animal sheds it and swells before the new one hardens.

items.p: Sort these animals by the kind of skeleton.
items: frog
Bones inside
crow
Bones inside
prawn
Exoskeleton
ant
Exoskeleton
earthworm
Hydrostatic skeleton
sea anemone
Hydrostatic skeleton
items.why: A frog and a crow have bones. A prawn and an ant have a hard outer covering. An earthworm and a sea anemone are held firm by liquid inside.

items.p: Put these in order, from a whole muscle down to its smallest part.
items: Muscle fibre
Actin and myosin threads
Muscle
Bundle of fibres
items.why: A muscle is made of bundles. A bundle is made of fibres, which are cells. Each fibre is packed with actin and myosin threads.

items.p: An earthworm's circular muscles contract. What happens to the segment?
items.why: The liquid inside keeps its volume. A segment squeezed thinner must get longer.

items.p: Which of these has no bone in it at all?
items.why: A tongue is almost all muscle. Thumb, jaw and heel each have bone.

items.p: Why does every muscle need a partner? Use the words 'pull' and 'long'.
items.a: A muscle can only pull by getting shorter. It cannot make itself long again. So something else, usually another muscle, must pull it long before it can work again.
items.why: A strong answer says that a muscle only shortens, and that the partner's job is to stretch it back.

items.p: In the Dough Worm, a roll was squeezed to half its width. What happened to its length, and why?
items.a: It became about four times as long. The amount of dough stayed the same. The roll got narrower from side to side and from top to bottom at once, so the dough had to spread along four times the length.
items.why: A strong answer gives 'about four times' and says that the amount of dough did not change.

items.p: Draw an arm twice: once bent and once straight. Colour the muscle that is contracted in each.
items.a: Bent arm: the biceps, on the front of the upper arm, is short and fat. Straight arm: the triceps, on the back, is short and fat. In each drawing the other muscle is long.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two muscles on opposite sides of the upper arm bone. Only one is short in each picture.
items.art: Two blank outlines of an arm from shoulder to hand, one bent and one straight.

worksheets.title: Inside the muscle and inside the joint (stretch)

items.p: Under a microscope, what happens to the threads inside a muscle fibre when it contracts?
items.why: The actin and myosin threads keep their length and overlap more. Scientists once thought they folded or coiled, and in 1954 two teams showed otherwise.

items.p: What does a myosin arm need in order to let go of actin?
items.why: ATP must arrive before the arm can release its grip. With no ATP, the arm stays locked on.

items.p: A body goes stiff some hours after death because the muscles have run out of ATP.
items.why: True. Without ATP the myosin arms cannot let go of actin, so the muscles lock. The stiffness passes when the threads begin to break down.

items.p: You lower a full bucket slowly into a well. Which arm muscle works hardest?
opts: The biceps, letting the arm down
The triceps, pushing the arm down
No muscle, because gravity does it
items.why: Gravity straightens the elbow. The biceps works to let the arm down slowly, so it works while it gets longer.

items.p: Cartilage has no ____ vessels, so it takes its food from the fluid in the joint.
items.why: Cartilage has no blood supply of its own. This is one reason why damaged cartilage heals slowly.

items.p: Match each part to what it does in a joint.
items.why: Each part has one main job. Together they let a joint move smoothly without coming apart.

items.p: Where are the muscles that bend and straighten your fingers?
items.why: Long tendons carry the pull from forearm muscles to the finger bones. You can feel the muscles work near your elbow when you wiggle your fingers.

items.p: At two main joints of a spider's leg, what straightens the leg?
opts: The pressure of the spider's blood
items.why: Those joints have a flexor muscle and no extensor. Liquid pushed into the leg under pressure straightens it, as Parry and Brown showed in 1959.

items.p: Put the steps of a moult in order.
items: The animal swells with water or air
The old exoskeleton splits
The new exoskeleton hardens
A new soft exoskeleton grows under the old one
The animal climbs out
a: A new soft exoskeleton grows under the old one
The animal swells with water or air
items.why: The new covering must be ready before the old one is shed. The animal swells while the new covering is still soft, so that it hardens at a larger size.

items.p: Three of these are muscular hydrostats. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: A crab's claw has a hard shell with muscles inside. The other three are almost all muscle, with no hard part.

items.p: A dough roll is 3 centimetres long. It is rolled to half its width. About how many centimetres long is it now?
items.why: Halving the width makes a roll about four times as long. 3 times 4 is 12 centimetres.

items.p: In the Finger Lift, the ring finger rose much higher when its neighbours were free. What does that tell you?
items.a: The ring finger is not simply weak. It is linked to its neighbours. Bands join the tendons on the back of the hand, so holding the neighbours down holds the ring finger down too.
items.why: A strong answer uses the evidence: the same finger went higher when only the neighbours changed.

items.p: A clam has one muscle to close the shell and no muscle to open it. How can the shell open?
items.a: A springy band at the hinge is squashed when the muscle closes the shell. When the muscle relaxes, the band springs back and opens the shell. The band is the muscle's partner.
items.why: A strong answer names something other than a muscle that undoes the pull, and says that it stretches the muscle again.

items.p: Draw one segment of an earthworm cut across. Show the circular muscle, the longitudinal muscle and the liquid.
items.a: A ring. The circular muscle is a thin layer round the outside, under the skin. The longitudinal muscle is a thicker layer inside it, seen as cut ends. The space in the middle is full of liquid, with the gut in the centre.
items.why: A strong drawing has two muscle layers round a space of liquid. Arrows may show that one layer squeezes round and the other pulls along.
items.art: A blank circle with a smaller circle in its centre.

items.p: Is an inside skeleton better than an outside one?

views.says: Inside is better. We can grow without ever losing our skeleton, and we can grow very big.
Outside is better. An insect gets armour and a skeleton in one. A hollow tube is light and stiff for a small body.
Neither is better. There are far more kinds of insect than kinds of animal with bones.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give one reason from this lesson. Then say one thing that is right in another view.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. For example: an exoskeleton must be moulted, and the animal is soft and in danger each time. But a tube on the outside is strong for its weight.
items.why: Each view has something right. A strong answer names a real gain and a real cost, such as armour and moulting.

items.p: A tongue gets a little narrower and thinner. What happens to its length?
opts: It grows by the same small amount
items.why: The volume stays the same. A small squeeze in two directions gives a large gain in length. That is why hydrostats can reach far and fast.

items.p: Why does a freshly moulted crab move so poorly?
opts: Soft tubes bend when muscles pull
The muscles have been shed too
The new shell is too heavy
items.why: A muscle needs something stiff to pull against. Until the new exoskeleton hardens, the tubes give way under the pull.

items.p: A plant has no muscles. How does a touch-me-not fold a leaf?
opts: Cells on one side let water out
items.why: Cells on one side of a swelling at the leaf base lose water quickly and go slack, so the leaf folds. The plant moves by changing a water skeleton.

items.p: When you hold your arm stiff, the biceps and the triceps are both pulling at once.
items.why: True. When both partners pull, neither wins, and the joint is held rigid. You can feel both muscles firm.

items.p: The elephant's trunk has one long bone down the middle.
items.why: False. A trunk has no bone. It is a muscular hydrostat, built from about 90,000 small bundles of muscle.

items.p: A joint of the skull that does not move is called a ____.
items.why: The plates of the skull lock together along zigzag sutures. They protect the brain and do not need to move.

items.p: Sort each pull by what undoes it.
cats: Something that is not a muscle
items: biceps bending the elbow
Another muscle
earthworm ring muscles
Another muscle
crab claw closing
Another muscle
spider leg bending
Something that is not a muscle
clam shell closing
Something that is not a muscle
biceps lifting a tumbler, then lowering it
Something that is not a muscle
items.why: The triceps, the worm's lengthwise muscles and the claw's opener are muscles. A spider's leg is straightened by liquid pressure, a clam is opened by a springy band, and gravity straightens the arm with the tumbler.

items.p: A dough roll 2 centimetres wide is 5 centimetres long. Rolled to 1 centimetre wide, about how many centimetres long is it?
items.why: Half the width gives about four times the length. 5 times 4 is 20 centimetres.

items.p: Scientists disagree about why no insect is as big as a dog. What should you say?
items.why: Oxygen supply, moulting, weight and being hunted by birds and bats have all been suggested. A 2026 study argued against the oxygen idea. It is honest to say the question is open.

items.p: Explain how you stick out your tongue, to someone who knows that muscles only pull.
items.a: Fibres that run across the tongue and from top to bottom contract. The tongue gets narrower and thinner. Its volume cannot change, so it gets longer and comes forward. A muscle from the chin also pulls the back of the tongue forward.
items.why: A strong answer has no pushing muscle in it. It uses the idea that the tongue keeps its volume.

items.p: Design a fair test: does a cold hand lift its fingers less high than a warm hand?
items.a: Measure the lift of each finger with the hand at room warmth. Hold the hand in cold water for one minute and dry it. Measure again in the same way, with the same ruler and the same helper. Do each measurement twice. Only the warmth of the hand changes.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing only, keeps the measuring the same, repeats each measurement and says what will be compared.

items.p: A friend says, 'My biceps bends my arm all by itself.' What would you add?
items.a: The biceps can bend the arm only if something has stretched it first, and that is the triceps or gravity. It also needs the bone to pull on, a tendon to join it to the bone, a nerve to switch it on and ATP from food.
items.why: A strong answer names the partner that stretches the biceps and at least one other thing the movement depends on.

items.p: Label the parts of this moving joint.
a: Bone: the two hard ends that meet
Cartilage: the smooth cap on each bone end
Synovial fluid: the liquid in the space between the caps
Ligament: the band that ties one bone to the other
items.why: The caps and the fluid let the bones slide. The ligaments stop them from coming apart.
items.art: A side view of a simple joint cut open: two bone ends with pale caps, a thin gap between them, a bag round the joint and a band at each side, with four blank label lines.

items.p: Draw a crab's leg as a tube. Draw the two muscles that bend and straighten the next joint.
items.a: A tube of shell with a second tube joined to it by a soft joint. Inside the first tube are two muscles, one fixed to each side of the next tube's base. One bends the joint and one straightens it.
items.why: A strong drawing puts both muscles inside the tube, on opposite sides of the joint.
items.art: A blank outline of two jointed tubes, like two sections of a crab leg.

items.p: Is the liquid inside an earthworm a skeleton?

views.says: No. A skeleton is hard. Water cannot be a skeleton.
Yes. It does the job of a skeleton. The muscles work against it, and it holds the body's shape.
It is half a skeleton. It only works because muscle and skin shut it in.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from the Dough Worm or the Water Balloon Worm. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason. For example: in the Water Balloon Worm, the water passed one pair of hands' squeeze to the other pair, which is what a bone does for two muscles. But the water did nothing until the balloon shut it in.
items.why: Scientists do call it a skeleton, because of the job it does. A strong answer says what job a skeleton does and tests the liquid against that.

quiz.p: Why can a muscle not push?
opts: Its threads can only slide together
quiz.why: The myosin arms drag the actin threads inwards. Nothing in the fibre can drive the threads apart again.

quiz.p: What stretches your biceps back to its long shape?
quiz.why: A muscle cannot lengthen itself. The triceps straightens the elbow and stretches the biceps. The weight of the arm can do it too.

quiz.p: Which joint is a ball and socket?
quiz.why: The round top of the thigh bone sits in a cup in the hip bone. The knee and finger joints are hinges.

quiz.p: Which kind of joint lets you shake your head to say no?
quiz.why: At the top of the neck, one bone turns round a peg on the bone below. That is a pivot.

quiz.p: What does cartilage do in a joint?
opts: Gives the bone ends a smooth cap
quiz.why: Smooth cartilage on smooth cartilage, wetted by synovial fluid, slides with very little friction. Ligaments tie bone to bone.

quiz.p: A beetle's leg muscles are where?
opts: Inside the hard tubes of the leg
On the outside of the shell
Only in the body, not the legs
quiz.why: A beetle has an exoskeleton. The muscles are inside it and pull on the inner side of the shell.

quiz.p: What is the biggest cost of an exoskeleton?
opts: The animal must moult to grow
quiz.why: A hard shell cannot grow. Each moult leaves the animal soft, slow and without armour for a time.

quiz.p: What is an earthworm's skeleton made of?
quiz.why: Each segment is a closed bag of liquid wrapped in muscle. The liquid keeps its volume, so the muscles can work against it.

quiz.p: A roll of dough is squeezed to half its width. How long does it become?
quiz.why: The roll gets narrower in two directions at once, so the same dough needs about four times the length. If you chose 'twice', remember that it also got thinner from top to bottom.

quiz.p: How does your tongue come out of your mouth?
opts: Muscles pull it thinner, so it gets longer
quiz.why: A tongue is a muscular hydrostat. Its volume stays the same, so when fibres pull it narrower and thinner it must lengthen.

quiz.p: Which of these is a muscular hydrostat?
quiz.why: An octopus's arm is almost all muscle, with no bone and no shell. A crab's leg has a shell, and a wing and a tail have bones.

quiz.p: In a fair test of finger lifting, what must stay the same for every finger?
quiz.why: Only the finger changes. The ruler, the helper, the hand position and the way of measuring stay the same, so the numbers can be compared.

applications: A physiotherapist treats a stiff or weak joint by working on both muscles of a pair. Strengthening one and stretching its partner go together.
Many artificial hands are worked by cords that run through the fingers like tendons. A motor in the palm or forearm pulls each cord, as a forearm muscle pulls a finger.
Engineers build soft robot arms with no rigid parts, copied from the octopus's arm and the elephant's trunk. Such an arm can wrap round a fragile object without crushing it.
The arm of an excavator at a building site is moved by oil pushed into cylinders under pressure. Liquid that keeps its volume carries the push, as it does in a spider's leg.
When the cartilage of a knee or a hip wears away, a surgeon can replace the joint surfaces with smooth metal and plastic.
Chitin from the shells of prawns and crabs is made into chitosan, a material used in some wound dressings.
Dancers, bowlers and veena players train both muscles of each pair, because smooth movement needs the partner to let go at exactly the right moment.

open_questions.q: Did muscle arise once in animals, or more than once?
open_questions.why_open: Jellyfish have striped muscle that looks like ours, but a 2012 study found it is built without some of our key proteins. That suggests it arose separately. Scientists are still comparing the genes of more animals.

open_questions.q: Why is no land insect as big as a dog?
open_questions.why_open: Oxygen supply, the danger of moulting with a heavy body, and being hunted by birds and bats have all been suggested. A 2026 study argued that oxygen is not the limit. No single answer is agreed.

open_questions.q: How does an octopus control an arm that can bend at any point?
open_questions.why_open: A bony arm has a few joints to control. An octopus's arm has no fixed joints. Most of her nerve cells are in the arms, and scientists are still working out how much each arm decides for itself.

open_questions.q: Can worn joint cartilage be made to grow back?
open_questions.why_open: Cartilage has no blood vessels and repairs itself very little. Researchers are trying cells grown in the laboratory and new materials, but no method yet rebuilds cartilage as good as the original.

open_questions.q: How much can practice free the ring finger?
open_questions.why_open: The links between the finger tendons are part of the hand's build. Musicians do gain finger control with training. How much of that is change in the brain's control, and whether the links themselves change, is not settled.

maths.problem: In a Dough Worm test, a roll was 4 centimetres long at the start. At half the width it measured 16 centimetres. How many times as long had it become?
maths.explain: Divide the new length by the starting length: 16 ÷ 4 = 4. The roll became 4 times as long.
maths.context: In the Dough Worm you roll a lump of dough thinner and measure how its length changes. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'four times as long' gives a rule that works for a lump of any size. '12 centimetres longer' would be true for this lump only.

maths.problem: Each time a dough roll is squeezed to half its width, it gets 4 times as long. A roll starts 4 centimetres wide and 3 centimetres long. How long is it at 1 centimetre wide?
maths.explain: From 4 centimetres wide to 2 is one halving: 3 × 4 = 12 centimetres. From 2 to 1 is a second halving: 12 × 4 = 48 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Dough Worm you find that halving the width of a roll makes it about four times as long.

chart.title: One lump of dough at three widths

maths.why_maths: A pattern lets you predict a result before you test it. This is how a small squeeze in a tongue or a tentacle can be known to give a long reach.

maths.problem: A child rolled a 4 centimetre long roll to 2 centimetres wide in the middle, and it measured only 12 centimetres, not 16. The ends were still fat. Explain the low result.
maths.answer: The fat ends held extra dough, so less dough was left to make length.
maths.explain: The rule needs the roll to be 2 centimetres wide all along. The fat ends were wider than that, so they held more than their share of dough. Rolled even, the roll would be longer.
maths.context: In the Dough Worm you roll dough to a set width and measure its length. The roll has to be the same width all along.
maths.why_maths: A number that does not fit the pattern is a clue. Working out why tells you what went wrong in the measuring.

maths.problem: In the Finger Lift, a ring finger lifted 1.4 centimetres on the first try and 1.8 centimetres on the second. What is the average?
maths.explain: Add the two tries: 1.4 + 1.8 = 3.2. Halve it: 3.2 ÷ 2 = 1.6 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Finger Lift you measure how high each finger can lift while the other four stay flat on the table. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: One try can be a fluke. The average of two tries is a fairer number to put on the chart.

maths.problem: A ring finger lifted 1.5 centimetres with its neighbours held flat, and 4.5 centimetres with them free. How many times as high is that? Does it fit the idea of a weak muscle?
maths.answer: 3 times as high. It does not fit a weak muscle.
maths.explain: 4.5 ÷ 1.5 = 3. The same muscle lifted the finger three times as high when only the neighbours changed. So the muscle was strong enough, and something was holding the finger back.
maths.context: In the Finger Lift you measure the ring finger twice: once with its neighbours held flat, and once with them free to rise. These are made-up results.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers tests an idea. If the muscle were weak, freeing the neighbours would change little.

maths.problem: A baby elephant's trunk has about 90,000 small bundles of muscle. A human body has about 600 named muscles. 90,000 ÷ 600 = 150. Why is '150 times as many muscles' not a fair claim?
maths.answer: Bundles and named muscles are different things, so the two numbers cannot be compared.
maths.explain: The sum is right: 90,000 ÷ 600 = 150. But one named human muscle, such as the biceps, is itself made of many bundles. The trunk number counts bundles and the human number counts whole muscles.
maths.context: An elephant's trunk has no bone. In 2023 scientists counted the small bundles of muscle in scans of a baby Asian elephant's trunk.
maths.why_maths: Before dividing two numbers, check that they count the same kind of thing. Otherwise a correct sum gives a wrong idea.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out what happens inside a muscle when it shortens? This card tells the true story of two teams and one week in 1954.
how_we_found_out.story: Under a microscope, a muscle fibre has dark and light stripes. By 1950 scientists knew that muscle holds two proteins, actin and myosin. Many thought that a muscle shortens because its long protein threads fold up or coil, like a spring closing. In 1953 Jean Hanson, a British scientist who was expert with a new kind of microscope, joined Hugh Huxley at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in America. Looking at rabbit muscle, they saw that the dark stripe, where the myosin lies, stays the same width when the muscle shortens. Only the light stripes get narrower. In Cambridge in England, Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke saw the same thing in living frog muscle. If the threads were folding, the dark stripe would shrink. It did not. So both teams proposed that two sets of threads slide past each other. Their papers were printed one after the other in the journal Nature on 22 May 1954. Few scientists were convinced at first. In 1957 Hugh Huxley's pictures showed tiny bridges between the two sets of threads, and the idea slowly won.
how_we_found_out.who: Jean Hanson and Hugh Huxley, and Andrew Huxley and Rolf Niedergerke
how_we_found_out.when: 1953 and 1954 for the two studies, 22 May 1954 for the two papers, and 1957 for the first clear pictures of the bridges
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a muscle shortens because its protein threads fold or coil up. The dark stripes of the fibre kept their width while the muscle shortened, so the threads were not getting shorter. They were sliding.
how_we_found_out.art: A woman in 1950s clothes looking down a microscope beside a drawing of a striped muscle fibre shown long and then short, with the dark stripes the same width in both.

roots.context: In this lesson you found that a muscle can only pull, and that a body gets longer when it is squeezed thinner. Here we ask what that tells us about who does the moving when a body moves.

deep_truth.truth: A muscle can only shorten, and it cannot make itself long again. In the Dough Worm, the dough grew four times as long when it was squeezed to half its width. An earthworm's ring muscles squeeze their own body like that, and the lengthening stretches the lengthwise muscles for their next pull. Bone, shell and liquid all do this one job: they carry one muscle's pull across to stretch another. So a skeleton is whatever lets muscles undo each other, and it need not be hard.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'my biceps bends my arm', as if one muscle did the job alone. We also use the word skeleton to mean bones. Both habits hide the same fact. A muscle is useless without a partner, and a skeleton is defined by what it does for the pair, not by what it is made of.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Dough Worm, a squeeze across became a push along. An earthworm has ring muscles and lengthwise muscles round liquid, and each set stretches the other. A spider's leg is bent by a muscle and straightened by liquid pressure. Under the microscope, muscle threads slide together and have no way to push apart.

three.who_am_i: When you bend your arm, the muscle that bends it was made ready by the muscle that straightens it. No part of you moves you alone.
three.what_is_life: Every animal who moves has the same problem, because muscle can only pull. Animals have solved it with bone, with shell, with liquid and with muscle itself.
three.what_is_this_world: A pull does nothing useful until something answers it. A rope needs a weight, a muscle needs a partner, and a worm's squeeze needs liquid that will not give way.

roots.thread: The threads inside a muscle can only slide together. From that one limit come very different bodies: your arm with two muscles and a bone, a crab with muscles inside a tube, a spider who straightens a leg with liquid, an earthworm whose skeleton is liquid, and a tongue that is its own skeleton. They look unlike, but each is the same arrangement, in which one pull is undone by an opposite pull. One rule shows up as many kinds of body. And inside each body, no muscle acts alone, so every movement is something the whole arrangement does.

teachings.teaching: Heraclitus says that people do not understand how a thing that pulls against itself agrees with itself. He calls it a fitting-together that turns back on itself, like that of a bow or a lyre.
teachings.link: A bow works only because the wood pulls one way and the string pulls the other. Your elbow works only because two muscles pull opposite ways. The opposition is what makes the movement possible.

teachings.teaching: The verse says that all actions are carried out by the qualities of nature. A person confused by the sense of 'I' thinks, 'I am the doer.'
teachings.link: The verse is about a person and their actions, not about muscles. But the science of this lesson shows something of the same shape in the body. We say one muscle bends the arm, when the bending is done by a pair, a bone, nerves and fuel together.

teachings.teaching: The chapter says that a person is soft and supple while alive, and stiff and hard when dead. It calls the stiff and hard the companions of death, and the soft and weak the companions of life.
teachings.link: A living muscle can let go, and letting go needs energy. A muscle with no energy left locks stiff. And two of the most skilful movers, an octopus's arm and an elephant's trunk, have no hard parts at all.

science.text: Actin and myosin are far older than muscles. Single-celled beings such as amoebas use the same two proteins to crawl and to divide. Animals built muscle from a tool that cells already had.

Whether muscle arose once or more than once in animals is still being worked out. A 2012 study found that the striped muscle of jellyfish lacks some key proteins that ours has. Its authors argue that such muscle arose separately in jellyfish and in animals like us.

other_view.view: Each muscle is a separate organ, with its own name, its own nerve and its own job. A doctor can test one muscle, find that it alone is weak, and repair it. On this view it is more useful, and more exact, to say 'the biceps bends the elbow' than to say that no muscle acts alone. And they would keep the word skeleton for hard parts, because a word that covers bone, water and tongue may be too wide to be useful.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was reasoned through step by step, as a parent and child would do it in a city flat. None of them has been tried at home yet, so treat the expected results as likely, not certain. The Dough Worm (core) needs only atta, a ruler and a piece of card. By the arithmetic of volume, a roll at half the width is four times as long. Hand rolling is uneven, so expect 14 to 18 centimetres where the rule says 16. Firm dough matters: sticky dough will not roll evenly, and dry dough cracks. The 1 centimetre roll is fragile, which is why that step uses a small lump. The Tongue Puzzle (core) needs a mirror, and the narrowing of the tongue is easy to see. In Who Is Working Now, the firm biceps during lowering is easy to feel with a full tumbler. In the Finger Lift, the ring finger usually lifts least, but hands differ, and a child who plays an instrument may find smaller differences. The Water Balloon Worm needs a balloon and is best done over a tray or in the bathroom, since a balloon can burst. Armour Up Close has a choice for families who do not cook prawns or crab: a shed insect skin or a live ant under a lens. In Droop and Rise, stalks droop within an hour on a hot dry day and may take longer than three hours in humid weather. A stalk that has dried too far may not rise again. The Bend Survey may show no pattern with only eight people, and the last step says so. In Build a Crab Claw, the usual first failure is a thread tied too close to the hinge. Facts were checked by web search while writing: the two 1954 papers on sliding threads and Jean Hanson's part, Kier and Smith's 1985 paper, Parry and Brown's 1959 spider paper, the 2023 count of trunk muscle bundles, the 2004 study of finger independence, the collagen structure from Madras in 1954, the coconut crab's size and its presence on the Nicobar Islands, the earthworm's muscles, the tongue's eight muscles, how the Kochi fishing nets work, and the three passages quoted in Roots. The three videos were confirmed by title and channel through YouTube's public lookup, but the videos were not watched. The 2026 study on insect size is known only from news reports of it.
